2d3b1882-9e60-4bdd-9ee2-e6df73b2bb07: Embodiment Practices is an invitation to practice giving ourselves permission to arrive fully to where we are, and gently explore movement and stillness to care for our bodies and ourselves. This event happens each week at the Alembic. As an element of self attunement, we will practice making intuitive choices through a lens of self love, meaning that we are each making choices that are nourishing and responsive to ourselves as individuals in that moment. Part of this practice includes being very intentional and explicit about what kinds of choices we might consider, and being curious about how it feels to try them. There will be many options provided throughout, with guidance around how to navigate choice making, including if this is new to you or you are navigating a limitation or injury. There will be a corner of the room set aside in case you’d like to opt out of the facilitated structure and take a moment for yourself to rest. Opening Circle: We'll ground and check-in with whatever feels present for each of us. We get to welcome ourselves to come as we are. Warm Up: We'll do a guided, full-bodied warm up, tuning the instruments of our bodies and attention, giving ourselves time to shake it out, stretch, wiggle, and move through whatever feels stuck. Movements will be simple enough to follow along, giving us a chance to get out of our heads and drop into our bodies, regulating our nervous system. Drawing on contemporary dance and yoga, there will be flow, rhythm, and music. Movement Explorations: We'll explore movements that deepen our connection with our bodies and our intuition, focusing on concepts and areas of the body that can help us settle and release. Meditation: Finally, we'll settle into meditation and rest. Finding stillness might be sitting/standing/lying down and might include cozy props, having eyes open or closed, and suggestions to make yourself comfortable, including allowing some body movement within that quiet space. Please bring clothes you feel comfortable to move in. It’s recommended to bring long sleeves, long pants and socks with you, in case we are moving on the floor. Bring a journal if you’d like. About Suzanne (Zan): With three decades of contemporary/modern dance experience and 15 years of teaching, Suzanne Beahrs guides students in exploring movement as a pathway to deeper connection—with ourselves, our surroundings, and each other. Her classes blend technical training, creative expression, and guidance on being intentional with how we are each practicing. Her movement style was described by The New York Times as “grounded, silken.” In addition to contemporary dance, she is currently heavily influenced by house dance, contact improvisation, and mindfulness practices. She is currently on faculty at Shawl-Anderson Dance Center and teaches around the Bay Area, including ODC, the Berkeley Alembic, and Finnish Hall. Zan has previously taught extensively at Gibney, Elon University, ADF studios, and many more. She has shown her choreography in NY, NC, CA, AZ, MA, and MO, and performed in works by Ishika Seth, Mo Miner, and others. Beyond the studio, Suzanne is a facilitator and has worked as a DEI consultant. She also enjoys exploring writing, visual art, nature, music, and belonging. Education: MFA in Dance, NYU Tisch School of the Arts; BA in Geology, UC Berkeley Learn more about Suzanne, upcoming classes/workshops (contemporary, embodiment, improvisation, contact improvisation and private lessons): IG @suzannebeahrs suzannebeahrs.com

03f29d7c-523b-46dd-aa84-ca4d7d1cdc8b: In January of 2024, local artist and author Dylan Miles was diagnosed with stage four appendix cancer. Though his prognosis was grim, Miles refused to give up and with the help of the Appendix Cancer Research Foundation he was able to receive a treatment called Cytoreduction Surgery and Hyperthermic Intraperitoneal Chemotherapy (CRS-HIPEC) which saved his life. Throughout the two difficult years from diagnosis through recovery Miles says that he made it through due to "community, movement, and art." Miles' 2026 memoir, My Not Chosen Adventure: A Medical Mystery and Love Story , is not just about his journey surviving cancer but also includes "rainbow squirrels and protective dragons." The book comes from Miles' "passion for open conversation about… hard stuff. And… a passion for joy and love and life." Miles will bring his unique, passionate perspective to the Main Library on Thursday, February 11th in conversation with our OPL librarian about the book and his journey. d22ffd99-88f2-4093-a019-198beb7cd42a: One of the defining Spanish instrumental artists of his generation · Vincen García is emerging as one of the defining Spanish instrumental artists of his generation, a musician with the virtuosity, identity and global ambition to push modern funk and fusion far beyond their traditional boundaries. Rooted in extraordinary musicianship but driven by the energy of contemporary culture, Vincen has developed a sound that brings together funk, jazz, fusion and rock with an immediacy rarely associated with instrumental music. His career has already taken him to some of the world’s most prestigious stages, including Montreux Jazz Festival in Switzerland, North Sea Jazz Festival in the Netherlands, Jazz in Marciac in France and Jazz in June in the United States, alongside sold-out performances and major appearances across Europe, the US and Asia. Yet what makes Vincen different goes far beyond technical ability. He represents a new kind of instrumental artist: charismatic, highly visual, digitally relevant and capable of connecting with audiences far outside the traditional jazz and fusion ecosystem. His live shows carry the intensity of a rock concert, while his music retains the sophistication, freedom and musicianship of the world’s finest instrumental artists. Through collaborations with internationally acclaimed musicians including Cory Wong (Vulfpeck), Nuno Bettencourt (Extreme), Cody Fry or Matteo Mancuso, Vincen has positioned himself at the heart of a new global generation reshaping instrumental music. If Paco de Lucía helped take flamenco from Spain to the world, Vincen García has the potential to become the Spanish artist who opens the door of modern funk and fusion to the mainstream. Not simply a bass player. Not simply a jazz artist. A global instrumental artist in the making.

cec49107-df0e-479e-ad79-64cd2430e8ea: One of the most brilliant and multifaceted musicians of our time · A protégé of the legendary Dizzy Gillespie, ARTURO SANDOVAL was born in Artemisa, Cuba, on November 6, 1949—just two years after Gillespie first introduced Latin influences into American jazz. From humble beginnings, Sandoval began studying classical trumpet at twelve, but it wasn’t long before the fire of jazz took hold. Today, he stands as one of the most brilliant and multifaceted musicians of our time: a virtuoso of trumpet and flugelhorn, a masterful pianist, timbalero, composer, and a fearless innovator whose artistry has captivated millions around the globe. Sandoval is renowned as one of the most dynamic performers alive. He has lit up the stage at the Oscars, the GRAMMY Awards, and the Billboard Awards, dazzling audiences with both breathtaking technique and sheer joy. The accolades match the legend: 10 GRAMMY Awards (19 nominations), 6 Billboard Awards, and an Emmy Award for composing the acclaimed underscore to HBO’s For Love or Country starring Andy Garcia. Widely recognized as one of the greatest trumpet players in history, Sandoval’s astonishing range, agility, and control allow him to execute the most intricate passages with power and emotion. His unique gift lies in his ability to seamlessly blend jazz, classical, and Latin traditions, creating a voice that is unmistakably his own. Beyond performance, he is a prolific composer, arranger, and educator, inspiring generations of musicians with his passion and dedication.

f7695b70-0f5a-4ac7-90a6-efb8e0d8903d: One of the most brilliant and multifaceted musicians of our time · A protégé of the legendary Dizzy Gillespie, ARTURO SANDOVAL was born in Artemisa, Cuba, on November 6, 1949—just two years after Gillespie first introduced Latin influences into American jazz. From humble beginnings, Sandoval began studying classical trumpet at twelve, but it wasn’t long before the fire of jazz took hold. Today, he stands as one of the most brilliant and multifaceted musicians of our time: a virtuoso of trumpet and flugelhorn, a masterful pianist, timbalero, composer, and a fearless innovator whose artistry has captivated millions around the globe. Sandoval is renowned as one of the most dynamic performers alive. He has lit up the stage at the Oscars, the GRAMMY Awards, and the Billboard Awards, dazzling audiences with both breathtaking technique and sheer joy. The accolades match the legend: 10 GRAMMY Awards (19 nominations), 6 Billboard Awards, and an Emmy Award for composing the acclaimed underscore to HBO’s For Love or Country starring Andy Garcia. Widely recognized as one of the greatest trumpet players in history, Sandoval’s astonishing range, agility, and control allow him to execute the most intricate passages with power and emotion. His unique gift lies in his ability to seamlessly blend jazz, classical, and Latin traditions, creating a voice that is unmistakably his own. Beyond performance, he is a prolific composer, arranger, and educator, inspiring generations of musicians with his passion and dedication.

04d46696-5a40-444d-af4e-d0dfed04ab1e: Every Tuesday morning, the Alembic opens for a half-day of silent meditation practice. This is an unguided silent retreat consisting of three 40-minute meditation periods. There will be no teacher-led instruction during the meditation periods. Participants are invited to bring and engage in their own silent meditation practice. Whether you practice mindfulness, Zen, Vipassana, contemplation, prayer, or another silent form of meditation, all are welcome. The retreat begins promptly at 9:30 AM and concludes at 11:50 AM. Please arrive between 9:15 AM and 9:25 AM to remove your shoes, settle in, and find a seat before the first bell. The morning is divided into three periods of silent meditation: 9:30 AM – 10:10 AM 10:20 AM – 11:00 AM 11:10 AM – 11:50 AM A bell will signal the beginning and end of each meditation period. The meditation hall (Sol) is reserved for silent practice during sitting periods. Between sits, participants may quietly stretch, visit the restroom, or spend time in the tearoom. Conversation is permitted during breaks; however, we encourage participants to keep voices low, as some attendees choose to observe silence throughout the entire morning. You are welcome to leave the meditation hall at any time if needed. If you leave during a meditation period, please wait until the next break before re-entering. We ask that all entrances and exits be as quiet and unobtrusive as possible. This is a “Bring Your Own Silent Meditation” retreat. We provide the structure and the space; you provide your own silent practice. Participants may choose to sit in Sol or engage in quiet movement practice in the tearoom during meditation periods. To minimize disruption, please enter Sol only during the transition periods between sits. If you arrive after a meditation period has begun, you are welcome to practice elsewhere in the Alembic until the next bell. The suggested donation is $10. No one will be turned away for lack of funds. We do ask that all attendees register through the Momence app or via the registration link on the Alembic website. Please note that the retreat ends at 11:50 AM, and we ask all participants to depart by 12:00 PM so that our volunteer teacher and staff may close the space in a timely manner. Thank you for helping us maintain a quiet and supportive environment for practice.
54bbf14d-0675-4b44-8156-462b64900f85: In this deeply experiential yoga practice, we will explore the dynamic interplay between stability and mobility, strength and relaxation, movement and stillness. Through mindful movement, standing and seated practices, breath, and attention to the subtle ways we organize ourselves in space, we'll investigate what allows us to feel both grounded and free. This event happens each week at the Alembic. Rather than striving for perfect alignment or mastering difficult poses, we'll approach the practice as an exploration. We'll slow down enough to notice, experiment with different possibilities, and discover how the balance between effort and ease can change our experience of movement — and of ourselves.. Teacher Bio: Vickie Russell Bell has been teaching yoga for more than 30 years, bringing together the precision of alignment-based yoga with a deep curiosity about how we inhabit our bodies, regulate our nervous systems, and move through the world. She is an E-RYT 500 and Certified Yoga Therapist (C-IAYT), and has studied with some of the most respected teachers in the Iyengar-influenced yoga tradition. Her teaching is grounded in the belief that yoga is less about mastering poses than developing a more intimate relationship with ourselves. Her classes invite students to slow down, pay attention, and explore the constantly shifting relationships between stability and mobility, strength and softness, effort and ease. She teaches students of all ages and abilities, with a particular interest in yoga as a practice for living fully and well over time.

60949e1e-c807-4ddb-adb9-d17a9e6a7265: It’s true that Berkeley-reared Charlie Hunter has long been a familiar presence on Bay Area stages. Even though he moved east decades ago and now resides in Greensboro, North Carolina, Hunter has maintained deep ties to his hometown. But the inveterately inventive 7-string guitar wizard has never presented anything quite like his trio with fellow guitar explorer Ella Feingold. Based in Western Massachusetts, she’s a pioneer of inverted tuning, which facilitates unexpected harmonic structures and voicings inaccessible in standard tuning. Inspired by the dauntingly prolific songwriter, jazz musician, and conceptual artist Chris Weisman, this approach shapes her signature sound—blending lush chord inversions, walking basslines, and expressive melodic phrasing, which makes Feingold a capaciously creative foil for Hunter. He’s hardly the only one seeking her out. She’s also been working with Meshell Ndegeocello, Bootsy Collins, and Erykah Badu (with whom she’s performed many times in the Bay Area). But it’s with Hunter that she’s defining her own musical identity. He’s carved out a major new role for himself over the past decade as a producer, and last year he released their debut album Different Strokes for Different Folks on his SideHustle label. Rooted in funk, jazz, soul and ambient textures, it’s a raw, spontaneous conversation between friends who find limitless new space to investigate deep in the pocket. Personnel: Charlie Hunter (guitar); Ella Feingold (guitar); TBA drums

4eb2a0dd-4d88-4ffa-986b-c9c4046685bd: Deconstructing Yourself is a weekly drop-in guided meditation (approximately one hour) plus Q & A with Berkeley Alembic founding teacher Michael Taft. Deconstructing Yourself is all about sharing the life-changing force that is meditation. We extend beyond any particular religion or technique in order to welcome any and all who are interested. Deconstructing Yourself strives to encourage, inform, and inspire your meditation practice towards ongoing awakening. Meditations are archived on YouTube here: https://www.youtube.com/michaeltaft108 Please arrive 10 minutes early. We do not allow any late entries for this event. Alembic founding teacher Michael W. Taft is a maverick meditation teacher, bestselling author, and podcaster. As a mindfulness coach, he specializes in secular, science-based mindfulness training in retreats, groups, corporate settings, and one-on-one sessions. Michael is the author of several books, including the bestselling The Mindful Geek, Nondualism: A Brief History of a Timeless Concept, and Ego (which he co-authored), as well as the editor of such books as Hardwiring Happiness by Rick Hanson and The Science of Enlightenment by Shinzen Young. He has often taught meditation at Google, worked on curriculum development for SIYLI, and is currently core faculty at Wisdom Labs, in San Francisco. Michael is also a featured teacher on the Simple Habit app, and an official advisor to the Therapeutic Neuroscience Lab. He was previously editor-in-chief of Being Human, and was the long-time editorial director of Sounds True. From Zen temples in Japan to yogi caves in India, Michael has been meditating for over thirty five years and has extensive experience in both Buddhist Vipassana and Hindu Tantric practice. Michael is a senior facilitator in Shinzen Young’s Unified Mindfulness system, and is a teacher of meditation groups around the Bay Area. f4cb5565-342b-4b91-bdb9-360878e18e66: Throwin’ Bo’s presents: Storefront Church Storefront Church is the project of Lukas Frank, who's drummed in Phoebe Bridgers' band and appeared on her albums, and the first song of his debut album As We Pass features DIIV frontman Cole Smith, but neither of those affiliations really prepares you for what to expect from As We Pass. It's a 9-song collection that's largely made up of bluesy, gothy, emo-y melancholic songs that sometimes sound like a cross between '90s Cure deep cuts and Nirvana Unplugged. (Lukas also cites Scott Walker as an influence, and you can hear that too.) Most of the album is bare-bones and somber, but Lukas also revs things up for the noise punk of "Faction from Under the Grove," and that fits right in too. With As We Pass, Lukas enters a long, line of depressive singer/songwriters, but even with over half a century of music like this, something about Lukas stands out. He grips you right off the bat with album opener "After the Alphabets" -- the kind of song that can make you drop everything and listen as soon as his voice comes in -- and the album stays that compelling throughout. Even with connections to established artists and the great Sargent House label behind him, this doesn't feel like the smash arrival of a hot new buzz artist; it's the subtle arrival of a songwriter whose songs creep up on you and knock you out when you're least expecting it. 3b4f8964-795f-4cfc-a9a6-ba394ef652cf: Imagery is one of the most important techniques for writing deep, meaningful fiction. With so much pressure on the language, images are like espresso beans, doing double or triple duty. Not only is there a concrete image, but there are also the associations that come with it. And the interpretations. And the subtext. For instance, in Shakespeare’s poem “Winter,” he writes, “birds sit brooding in the snow,” and from there, the word associations begin to multiply: flight, flying, wings, air, sky, nest, and so on. By reading published short stories with close attention, we’ll see how imagery provides specificity, creating a sensory experience for the reader and also proliferating meanings that are not explicitly on the page. We’ll see how images can infuse the plot and shape the character arc; they can express the story’s main theme largely through metaphor. We’ll see how an image can have its own arc of change, collecting different meanings like a magnet. We’ll learn how concrete details can lead to mystery and, when connected to other images, eventually lead to revelation. Writing prompts generated from the published stories will help us put these techniques into practice, drafting writing with images that add deep dimensions to your stories. e77e4430-2508-4891-a933-10877f5a937d: Creative expression is a way to integrate phenomenon and visions experienced in altered states of consciousness, whether they be meditative or entheogenic in nature. From the very first forms of mark-making to the caves of Lascaux to the works of Pablo Amaringo and Alex Grey, humanity has sought to understand our internal landscapes through visual expression. Alligator Lizards in the Air: Healing and Integration through Creative Expression, is a once a month chance to bring these experiences to life through two dimensional mark making. Art mediums from paint to colored pencils, crayons to markers, will be available for everyone to use along with paper and canvas. Krisztina Lazar will be your visionary guide in creativity and will help you realize your experience before your eyes. No art background needed for this class. All you need is an open mind and a willingness to explore. No one turned away for lack of funds. If this applies to you, please email hello@berkeleyalembic.org at least 48 hours before the event start. Krisztina Lazar is a visionary artist primarily working in oil paint, watercolor and drawing. She is a Mische Technique lineage holder, a mixture of oil and egg tempera painting invented during the Dutch Renaissance and revolutionized by modern master, Ernst Fuchs. This technique creates an opalescent under painting that the colors are then glazed over, rendering each painting out of light rather than shadow, bringing the images to life with fractal clarity. Utilizing this transformative style that she learned from visionary pioneer, Brigid Marlin, her current body of work explores painting a hybrid of Mische and Alla Prima to render hyperealistic sacred art. With these two techniques combined, Krisztina creates images of Pop Shamanism, portals and visions that speak to today’s cultural climate of the occult, magic, fantasy, psychedelics, meditation, pop, nostalgia, and the environment movement. Originally from Cleveland, OH, she completed her BFA at Carnegie Mellon University in 2004 and her MFA graduate degree in 2011 at the San Francisco Art Institute New Genres department. Her paintings have been exhibited in group and solo shows throughout the United States and Europe, most notably at the H.R. Geiger museum in Gruyere, Switzerland. She teaches her unique styles of painting to many students in group and private settings. Her work has been featured in multiple articles, galleries and book publications. She currently lives and works in Northern California.

1f65d5c5-4185-4a6e-8ec0-c6f5d9201f26: Guitar music with a mix of Spanish, Mexican, and World elements · Ottmar Liebert’s global success can be attributed to a myriad of things – his creative vision, his determination, and a strong sense of melody. Born in Cologne, Germany, he began playing guitar at 11. Before the age of 19, Liebert had intended to stay in Germany and pursue a career as a designer and photographer. However, while journeying extensively through Asia and playing with other travelers and local musicians, he realised that he could not escape a life of music. After pursuing his dreams of playing rock music in Boston, he settled in Santa Fe, New Mexico. Santa Fe was a fresh start for Liebert in many ways, and in addition to returning to the acoustic guitar, he remained open to letting the place define the music he made. It was this openness to the local landscape that defined what was to become his musical style, a mix of Spanish, Mexican, and World elements, strong melodies tinged with a shade of melancholy, balanced with upbeat rhythms. Liebert founded the first incarnation of his band, Luna Negra, in 1989. His debut album began as a self-produced release called Marita: Shadows and Storms, copies of which local Native American artist Frank Howell distributed in his art galleries. After the record made its way to radio stations, it began generating a buzz among programmers and received an unprecedented response among listeners. Higher Octave Music picked it up and released a fully remastered version, Nouveau Flamenco. Recorded for less than $3,000 on an old analog machine in a shack beside a gravel pit, this CD became an international sensation, establishing Liebert’s unique border-style flamenco, and becoming the best-selling instrumental acoustic guitar album of all time: 2 x Platinum – USA 14 x Platinum – USA/Latin Platinum – Australia Platinum – New Zealand Gold – Canada Gold – Mexico Visual art has always been essential to Ottmar Liebert’s world-view and even today he is an avid photographer. “My music is visual,” Liebert says. “Santa Fe has great light, that special thing you get in the high desert. Some days you can see for 100 miles, and think you can reach into the sky or walk off a ridge and keep flying. That’s how I felt when I recorded Nouveau Flamenco.” Liebert has since become one of the most successful instrumental artists of the past decades, entertaining audiences around the world and releasing a catalog of 33 classic albums including live recordings, an orchestral album for Sony Classical, a binaural surround sound recording, remix albums, a lullaby and a flamenco-reggae album. During his career, he has played more than two thousand concerts worldwide. Ottmar Liebert and Luna Negra have played two concerts with the New Mexico Philharmonic featuring Liebert’s music arranged by bassist Jon Gagan. These two concerts, to date, have broken attendance records for the New Mexico Philharmonic. Ottmar Liebert has been nominated for five Grammy awards. Of Liebert’s thirty-three albums, there are some that stand out. Borrasca (1991) was Grammy nominated, but it is exceptional in Liebert’s mind for another reason. Although everyone wanted him to make another Nouveau Flamenco, this album went in a different direction. He added horns and piano, giving the album a different vibe and sound. Solo Para Ti (1992) featured two songs on which Carlos Santana played. Santana’s was the first concert Ottmar Liebert ever attended, and he was a huge influence on Liebert’s melodic playing. The Hours Between Nights + Day (1993), nominated for a Grammy, mixed the Japanese koto with the flamenco guitar; on this album, Liebert used his electric guitar for the first time since the mid-eighties, and combined programmed drums with live percussion. He also ingeniously layered field recordings with the original music, creating a musical odyssey that is dreamy and atmospheric. The album contains the only Spanish-language version of the Marvin Gaye hit Mercy, Mercy Me Opium (1996), again nominated for a Grammy, was the first album recorded in Liebert’s new studio in Santa Fe. Liebert received many accolades for this album from fans around the world and emails and letters from listeners describing how evocative Opium was. La Semana (2004) was the first album Liebert engineered by himself. It was the first time there was no sound engineer on the “other side of the glass,” and Liebert discovered that at first, he played what he had planned but then after he dropped this, it was just “pure play”. One Guitar (2006), also nominated for a Grammy, was a milestone album for Ottmar Liebert in that it was his first solo guitar album. Waiting n Swan (2015) is special to Liebert because to him it reconnects two branches of rhythm – tangos, flamenco and reggae, proving that there is no such thing as “purity” in music. slow (2016) is an album that Liebert felt it was incumbent upon him to make a statement against the sound of billions of smartphones beeping with the latest news, likes, and comments, keeping us in a state of constant alarm. His album is framed around the notion that a slow tempo can change listeners’ heartbeats and blood pressure.

Waiting n Swan (2015) is special to Liebert because to him it reconnects two branches of rhythm – tangos, flamenco and reggae, proving that there is no such thing as “purity” in music. slow (2016) is an album that Liebert felt it was incumbent upon him to make a statement against the sound of billions of smartphones beeping with the latest news, likes, and comments, keeping us in a state of constant alarm. 879dad20-d612-4581-8b9c-270bc9d7ac28: From two leading scholars, a concise, authoritative work naming and explaining a bigotry that is usually misunderstood or outright ignored. For decades, the voices of Palestinians and those who advocate for Palestinian rights have been stifled—if not outright silenced—in the United States, according to scholars Ussama Makdisi and Saree Makdisi. More recently, activists have been arrested by federal agents merely for writing op-eds, while pro-Palestinian speech in universities as well as media and civic institutions has faced an unprecedented crackdown. How are we to understand this intolerance in the supposed land of the free? In Anti-Palestinianism , the Makdisis, two of the most prominent Palestinian American scholars in the United States, argue that the phenomenon is not reducible to Islamophobia or to general anti-Arab animus. Rather, they show that anti-Palestinianism constitutes a distinct form of bias rooted in the specific historical and political circumstances of Palestine and Israel—it is an attempt to deny the Palestinian story altogether through an unprecedented system of assumptions, norms, rules, and even laws. Drawing on a vast array of historical examples, the Makdisis have produced an essential work that gives language and clarity to the limits of American inclusion. How is it possible for the Palestinians to openly dispossessed, subjugated, starved and massacred while the world's liberal democracies watch on and do almost nothing to save them? Saree and Ussama Makdisi provide a well-argued and brilliantly nuanced answer to that question in this brave, timely and hugely important book. They minutely dissect the way the Palestinian people have been dehumanised and their lives devalued over the course of a century, their very existence erased, so preparing the way for their ethnic cleansing and genocide. Anti-Palestinianism is essential reading to understand the biggest moral issue of our time. — William Dalrymple Saree and Ussama Makdisi have written a groundbreaking book that grippingly and thoroughly delineates the massive and relentless machinery behind anti-Palestinianism in the West: a deadly bigotry we need to and will overcome. Anti-Palestinianism will shock and inspire you. It is a foundational work, and should be read in every house, taught in every classroom. — Fady Joudah, author of Exhibit G Racism always substitutes real people and their history for phantoms and monsters. But when those monsters are Palestinian, slaying them is considered a noble and necessary act to protect Jews, while condemning genocide of Palestinians is somehow antisemitic. In this timely and devastating book, Saree and Ussama Makdisi break down the logic of anti-Palestinianism, its settler colonial roots, its ties to other racial regimes, and its enablers in the liberal media, academia, and much of the international community. The authors are clear: dismantling the colonial and racial order are preconditions for a Free Palestine, and a genuinely free world. — Robin D. G. Kelley, author of Freedom Dreams: The Black Radical Imagination If Americans are like fish, anti-Palestinianism is like water—so ubiquitous it remains largely invisible. Naming it, so Americans recognize how often our public debates assume that Palestinian lives matter less than Jewish ones, is crucial work. This is a genuinely important book. — Peter Beinart, author of Being Jewish After the Destruction of Gaza This book patiently and brilliantly deconstructs the greatest fallacy of our era: that those who struggle against Israeli settler colonialism and for Palestinian freedom are by definition antisemitic. Saree and Ussama Makdisi, two of the most prominent Palestinian intellectuals of our present, identify the engine of Zionist genocidal violence in a form of racism they define as anti-Palestinianism, manifested in the negation of Palestinian identity, history, and experience. Now erupting in full force, this form of racism seeks to negate Palestinian life itself. The book thus calls us to confront anti-Palestiniansm as the most urgent and essential condition for a politics of resistance and liberation. — Eyal Weizman, author of The Ungrounding Saree Makdisi is professor of English and comparative literature at the University of California, Los Angeles. He is a scholar of imperial culture and has written extensively about Palestine. Ussama Makdisi is a professor of history and the May Ziadeh Chair of Palestinian & Arab Studies at the University of California, Berkeley. He was previously the first Arab American Educational Foundation Chair of Arab Studies at Rice University. f56deead-1561-4e81-abf2-7a783b98d7d1: A group meditation/authentic relating practice that explores what is coming up in the present moment as we relate to each other Welcome to a twice-monthly drop-in Relatefulness practice with Josh Rosenberg and Daniel Ricciardelli. Relatefulness is an exploration of what is coming up in the present moment as we relate to the others in the group. It is a close friend of relational practices like Circling™, Authentic Relating, and T-Group, with slightly more emphasis on group interaction and flexibility in how to express what is arising in the present moment. This is a mixed-levels event. Beginners are welcome and will be supported with tools to aid their exploration. Advanced practitioners will be challenged to find the next edge of their practice. We cap attendance for the event at 15 people. If you want to be sure to be able to join, purchase your ticket in advance! What We’ll Explore Through paired, small group, and full group processes, we will practice: Noticing and naming the content of our experience, including: our emotions, body sensations, and present moment reactions to others in the group. Noticing and naming the context of our experience, including: our assumptions, the norms of the group, and projections onto one another and society. Revealing our experience to one another to help all of us see each other and our broader social reality more clearly. Leading the group in the direction we want to go. This is a practice where all participants are invited to notice their desires for the group and to practice directing the group by embodying the kinds of expression they want to see more of. Why Come? You may be looking to: Cultivate more authentic, nourishing relationships, where you can be yourself and stay connected. Take your insights about personal growth and explore them in an interpersonal context. Set clear, compassionate boundaries instead of repeating painful patterns This practice helps to develop skills that support all of the above. Also, it's fun! What Not to Expect This is not a therapy session or group healing experience, although healing can occur. It’s a group exploration of what is arising in the present moment. This naturally tends to bring out more truth and love in the group, but there is not a particular goal or endpoint we are trying to reach. Here’s what NOT to expect: A space free of conflict or triggers. When people are open about what's coming up in their experience, things can get edgy sometimes! We don’t view being triggered as inherently negative, but rather a natural part of the human experience that can be rich to explore. We aim for a space where safety grows from honesty and genuine care, not from avoiding interpersonal conflict. To support this, we will establish some boundaries up front, such as asking for explicit consent before making physical contact with others. No enforced hierarchy of emotions. Beauty, awkwardness, boredom, anger, and joy are all welcome. Each experience has worth, and none automatically justify themselves as more important. Expression without attunement. We value honest expression, and we also stay attentive to its impact on others. This is a space for mindful connection, not expression at any cost. Facilitators may pause or redirect moments that move away from relational presence. Other logistics and notes Participants enter the space at 6:30 and we close the doors for the event at 6:35. Please arrive on time! We hope to see you at a future event! Feel free to reach out to jhrosenberg [at] gmail [dot] com or dbricciardelli [at] gmail [dot] com if you have questions about whether this event is a fit for you. More about the facilitators Josh Rosenberg (he/him) is a certified facilitator through the Relateful Company training program. He has hosted and facilitated weekly relatefulness sessions for small groups for several years while continuing to grow his practice through retreats and regularly engaging other facilitators. Josh loves exploring what's honestly coming up in the present moment in a group of people, and the novelty and relief it tends to bring. When he's not leading relatefulness sessions or at work, you may find him loving the heck out of music, movies, and comedy, participating in Michael Taft's meditation courses, or passionately following the New York Jets football team despite its many flaws. In his day job, Josh is CEO at the Forecasting Research Institute, a nonprofit aiming to advance the science of forecasting and increase its policy-relevance. Daniel Ricciardelli (he/him) has hundreds of hours in relational awareness practices of various forms, and is a certified Relatefulness practitioner through the Relateful Company. A virtuoso known for his dazzling improvisations and genre-defying musicality, Tolling spent nine years with the Grammy-winning Turtle Island Quartet, toured internationally with legendary bassist Stanley Clarke, and most recently performed with Bob Weir & Wolf Bros as part of the Wolf Pack. Kenny Washington, renowned for his extraordinary four-octave range, impeccable phrasing, and electrifying stage presence, is one of the most exciting jazz vocalists performing today. Tony Lindsay, the 11-time Grammy-winning former lead singer of Santana, brings his unmistakable soulful voice and infectious energy to the stage. Together, these three powerhouse performers will explore beloved jazz standards, soul classics, and unexpected musical gems, with plenty of spontaneous interplay. Joining them is an outstanding rhythm section featuring John R. Burr on piano, Dan Feiszli on bass, and Eric Garland on drums. A rare musical collaboration, six extraordinary musicians, and one spectacular night at Yoshi’s Oakland!
149a6bef-3b02-4a78-9657-f0c5ffc7e540: A father sets out to build the perfect daughter. With the help of a scientist, he creates an AI version of Claudia, adjusting her life again and again in pursuit of something just right. But each new iteration brings unexpected results. The more he tries to control who she becomes, the more complicated she gets. By turns hilarious and deeply revealing, Chloé Hung’s Perfect Daughter explores the gap between expectation and reality, and the quiet heartbreak of trying to be seen, understood, and loved on your own terms.

27030d2f-8735-43dd-88cb-1e1effcd39b5: “A bundle of energy that expertly marries the organic and synthetic” (Everything is Noise), the electro-acoustic fusion juggernaut Sungazer is the brainchild of bass virtuoso Adam Neely and mind-bending drummer Shawn Crowder. From the outset, Sungazer has challenged the boundaries separating jazz fusion, progressive rock, and electronic production, creating music that feels simultaneously cerebral and visceral. Neely’s elastic bass lines weave through Crowder’s hyper-detailed polyrhythms with astonishing precision, yet the duo never sacrifices groove for technicality. Instead, their compositions thrive on tension and release, balancing virtuosic complexity with infectious melodies and digitally inspired textures. Against the Fall of Night represents the clearest realization of Sungazer’s artistic philosophy to date. Across the album, shimmering synthesizers collide with explosive drumming, while intricate rhythmic modulations transform each track into an unpredictable sonic journey. By combining internet-age electronic aesthetics with improvisational sophistication, the band has carved out a singular identity that continues reshaping expectations for contemporary instrumental music. Their fearless experimentation ensures fusion remains innovative, relevant, and resonant. Personnel: Adam Neely (bass); Shawn Crowder (drums); Others TBA

1e040553-65ca-4b3f-ab7a-5403c9f51a35: Psychedelics can surface anything, including awe, insight, grief, trauma, even ancestral or collective pain. Without support, it can be hard to make sense of what happened, let alone carry it forward in a meaningful way. Yirah—often translated as awe, reverence, or a kind of holy trembling—is the feeling of standing at the edge of something vast, meaningful, and not entirely knowable. Psychedelic experiences often bring us right to that edge. This Jewish psychedelic integration circle offers a space to meet those moments together, within the safety of Jewish community and the container of Jewish teachings. Together, we make meaning of what we’ve seen and felt, and begin the slow, human work of weaving those insights into our lives. Please arrive 10 minutes early to get settled in. We’ll begin promptly at the scheduled start time and cannot accommodate late arrivals. Thank you for helping us create a smooth experience for everyone. Each monthly, drop-in circle includes grounding and intention-setting, a brief orientation, an experiential practice (meditation, movement, somatic work, or parts work), and small- and large-group sharing. This is a supported peer group rather than psychotherapy, designed to foster connection, reflection, and practical integration. Note: This is an affinity space exclusively for people who identify as Jewish—by heritage or conversion—including those who are part-Jewish. Those who do not meet these criteria will not be admitted. To support safety and connection in a time of deep division, we also hold a clear and intentional container: we do not engage in political discussion here. The focus is on integration, presence, and community. Whether you’re new to Jewish practice or finding your way back in, whether your journeys have been expansive, messy, or disorienting—you’re welcome here. Facilitator Bio: Lyssa Menard, PhD, is a clinical psychologist, psychedelic therapist, and professor at Northwestern University Medical School who specializes in trauma, integrative medicine, and what it actually takes to change. She’s been featured in places like CNN and The New York Times, but her real work happens in circles like this one—where people show up as they are and do the brave, uncomfortable, life-changing work of integration. Jewish by birth and in a more recent, intentional deep dive into Jewish life, Lyssa brings a deep respect for tradition alongside a willingness to question, wrestle, and reinterpret—in the long Jewish tradition of meaning-making. After all, Israel can be translated as “one who wrestles with God.” Her relationship to psychedelics is both professional and personal. She’s experienced their power, their limitations, and everything in between—which makes her equal parts skeptic and believer.

67edda27-988a-473f-a388-c44d52472249: Topic and guest to be announced. The Chalice is a recurring psychedelic salon held at the Berkeley Alembic the first Wednesday of every month. Instead of the mainstream focus on clinical trials, legal frameworks, and psychotherapy, the Chalice will draw from the deeper humanistic wells of history, poetry, the gods, ethnobotany, humor, and mystery. We are less interested in fetishizing psychedelic substances or psychedelic experiences than in cultivating psychedelic culture and exploring what it means to be psychedelic people. This first half of this event will be streamed online. The co-hosts for Chalice are Erik Davis, author and Alembic co-founder; Maria Mangini, co-founder of the Women’s Visionary Council and old-school head; and Christian Greer, currently a lecturer on counterculture at Stanford University. The first half of each gathering will feature a talk or special guest interview; the second half of the evening is designed to develop the community, sometimes with breakout groups, story hours, and peer-to-peer discussion, and always with more questions than answers. J. Christian Greer, PhD, is a scholar of Religious Studies with a special focus on global psychedelic culture. He has held teaching positions at Harvard University, Yale University, and is currently a lecturer at Stanford's Medical School. He is the co-founder, and the co-chair of the Drugs and Religion program unit at the American Academy of Religion, and each June, he leads “The Psychedelic Universe: Global Perspectives on Higher Consciousness,” an intensive, 2-week seminar on the history of psychedelics, hosted on-location at the University of Amsterdam, Netherlands. Alongside his research, he is an organizer for the Order of St. George's Horse, a pilgrimage confraternity & book publisher. His latest books include, Void Machines: the Paper Shrines of J. Christian Greer is a collection of his artwork, and Kumano Kodo: Pilgrimage to Powerspots (co-authored with Dr. Michelle Oing) which analyzes the pilgrimage folklore associated with the rainforests of Japan's Kii Peninsula. Learn more about his work here: orderofstgeorgeshorse.com Erik Davis, PhD, is an author, award-winning journalist, and teacher based in San Francisco. His wide-ranging work focuses on alternative religion, media culture, the popular imagination, and the psychedelic underground. He is the author of High Weirdness: Drugs, Esoterica, and Visionary Experience in the Seventies (2019); Nomad Codes: Adventures in Modern Esoterica (2010); The Visionary State: A Journey through California’s Spiritual Landscape (2006), a critical volume on Led Zeppelin (2005), and the celebrated cult classic TechGnosis: Myth, Magic, and Mysticism in the Age of Information (1998), which remains in print. Davis’s scholarly and popular essays on music, technoculture, drugs, and spirituality have appeared in scores of books, magazines, and journals, and his writing has been translated into a dozen languages. Davis has spoken widely at universities, conferences, retreat centers, and festivals, and has been interviewed by CNN, the BBC, NPR, and the New York Times. He graduated from Yale University in 1988, and earned his PhD in religious studies at Rice University in 2015. He writes the online publication the Burning Shore (www.burningshore.com), and his next book is Blotter: the Untold Story of an Acid Medium (2024).www.techgnosis.com Mariavittoria Mangini, PhD, FNP has written extensively on the impact of psychedelic experiences in shaping the lives of her contemporaries, and has worked closely with many of the most distinguished investigators in this field. She is one of the founders of the Women’s Visionary Council, a nonprofit organization that supports investigations into non-ordinary forms of consciousness and organizes gatherings of researchers, healers, artists, and activists whose work explores these states. She is a visiting scholar at the Berkeley Center for the Science of Psychedelics, and Professor Emerita in the School of Science, Allied Health, and Nursing at Holy Names University. For the last 50 years, she has been a part of the Hog Farm, a well-known communal family based in Berkeley and in Laytonville, California.

83b2bf9e-a253-43e3-b43a-f7ee24e57084: For his second night of the season, trumpeter Ambrose Akinmusire performs with his long-term working quartet including pianist Sam Harris, bassist Harish Raghavan, and drummer Justin Brown — the group with which he made his first SFJAZZ appearance as a leader in 2011. To the jazz world, Akinmusire’s ascension from young Oakland-born trumpeter at Berkeley High School to one of the most important voices in jazz seemed shockingly brief. In truth, his trajectory has been a linear progression, starting in earnest with a touring opportunity from influential saxophonist and composer Steve Coleman while still in high school, and built on a foundation of study at the Manhattan School of Music and the Thelonious Monk Institute of Jazz at USC with Herbie Hancock, Wayne Shorter, and Terence Blanchard. After decamping to New York, Akinmusire built his résumé as a sideman with the likes of Vijay Iyer and Aaron Parks, and in 2007, won both the prestigious Carmine Caruso International Jazz Trumpet Solo Competition and the star-making Thelonious Monk International Trumpet Competition. Since then, the trumpeter has been a whirlwind of activity but has always returned to this quartet as home base, heard most recently on 2020’s GRAMMY-nominated On the Tender Spot of Every Calloused Moment. Personnel: Ambrose Akinmusire (trumpet); Sam Harris (piano); Harish Raghavan (bass); Justin Brown (drums)

6dfdb57b-48be-4e83-9a62-9fe329d6de75: The GRAMMY-winning Jewish klezmer superstars celebrate 40 years of music with this performance of material from their new album, We Were Made For These Times — a powerful new body of work rooted in protest, hope, and resilience. Formed in New York’s East Village in 1986, the Klezmatics led the resurgence of the nearly forgotten klezmer tradition and contemporized it with an irreverent dose of punk rock attitude, and since their inception, have been one of most visible faces of today’s Yiddish culture. Enduring a number of personnel changes over the past two decades, the band has revolved around original members Lorin Sklamberg on lead vocals and accordion, trumpeter/keyboardist Frank London and bassist Paul Morrissett. They have collaborated with violin virtuoso Itzhak Perlman, Pulitzer Prize winner Tony Kushner and Israeli vocalist Chava Alberstein, and have released a dozen diverse albums, including the GRAMMY-winning Wonder Wheel, their first session that set previously unused Woody Guthrie lyrics to their own original material. The band would expand their integration of Guthrie’s words to new compositions on their Happy Joyous Hanukkah and Happier Joyous Hanukkah projects that have been an SFJAZZ holiday tradition for many years. Released on International Workers’ Day in 2026, We Were Made For These Times brings together Jewish, Black gospel, Latin American, Crimean Tatar, and avant-jazz voices, creating a shared musical language of solidarity for the world we are living in now. Personnel: Lorin Sklamberg (lead vocals, accordion, guitar, piano); Matt Derriau (kaval, clarinet, saxophone); Lisa Gutkin (violin, vocals); Frank London (trumpet, keyboards); Paul Morrissett (bass, tsimbl); Richie Barshay (percussion)

Each rhythm - Flowing, Staccato, Chaos, Lyrical, and Stillness, is a gateway, a wisdom teacher guiding us toward greater presence, healing, and transformation. This event occurs every two weeks at the Alembic. In a Sweat Your Prayers®, we support your individual practice with the rhythms and your movement journey by dancing wave after wave with light guidance. People often leave feeling cleansed, grounded, more alive, and more connected to themselves and their deeper knowing. 5Rhythms® is for every body. Many have discovered that not having prior dance training is actually liberating! Bring your body temple and a willingness to be surprised by what's waiting to move in and through you. The dance will end around 12:15pm, followed by a closing circle until around 12:30-ish. We encourage spacious arrivals and unhurried departures. Teacher Bio: Qibei is a 5Rhythms® teacher, mindfulness teacher, holistic healer, and Associate Marriage and Family Therapist, though no title could fully capture the many worlds she moves between. Her work bridges the clinical and the mystical, the tender and the fierce, the grounded intelligence of the body and the mystery of Spirit moving through human life. For over 20 years, alongside 5Rhythms®, her path has been richly shaped by Continuum Movement, Open Floor, somatic contemplative practice, and relational communication. Over time, these disciplines began weaving together into the way she listens, guides, and teaches. For Qibei, dance is medicine, prayer, and creative laboratory, a place where we can move beyond numbness, habitual defenses, and rigid identities we’ve learned to carry, and reconnect with our raw aliveness and deeper knowing. In her movement spaces, Qibei creates a trauma-sensitive and inclusive field for all bodies, inviting authentic expression and the dynamic interplay between body, heart, psyche, and spirit. Her music and facilitation are often described as exquisite, nourishing, and deeply transporting, guiding movers into inner landscapes they didn’t know they could reach. 4e60bbeb-c958-4fa5-a2ed-f6efe4980b46: Many of us work with psychedelics without a guide or with limited support to integrate these experiences. That can feel painful or lonely when we’ve had meaningful journeys (and also when we’ve had disappointing journeys!). Healing – especially from interpersonal injuries – deepens when done in community. The same is true of personal and spiritual growth. Even the most joyful experiences are best metabolized when witnessed. Together, we become a mosaic – a colorful and varied community, greater together than the sum of our parts. Mosaic is a psychedelic integration circle for self-identified women. Here, you’ll find a supportive space to integrate the lessons, challenges, and wisdom from psychedelic journeys so that you can apply those learnings to everyday life. Together, we’ll seek to understand our psychedelic experiences and make profound insights accessible and actionable. Please arrive 10 minutes early to get settled in. We’ll begin promptly at the scheduled start time and cannot accommodate late arrivals. Thank you for helping us create a smooth experience for everyone. This is a drop-in, monthly supported peer group rather than a psychotherapy group. We create space for sharing stories and experiences, receiving support, and forging genuine connections. Meditation, mindful movement, somatic practices, Internal Family Systems parts work, and creative tools are all part of the fun. Whether you’re new to integration or looking to deepen your practice, you’ll find a supportive community here. Note: You’re invited to bring an object for our community altar that represents some aspect of your journey. No one turned away for lack of funds. If this applies to you, please pay at the door. Dr. Lyssa Menard is a psychologist, psychedelic therapist, and professor (Northwestern University Medical School) with specialties in Integrative Medicine, trauma treatment, and health psychology. f5ee7406-837c-4715-9b12-c689f218cb88: October Theme: “Broadway and Show Tunes” There’s nothing that brings people together better than singing our favorite songs. It recalls summer nights around the campfire: someone strumming the guitar and all singing a mix of folk music, familiar songs we heard on the radio, and occasional new songs that someone shares. Nobody has to worry about whether you know the songs or can sing like a pro. This is our chance to share the joy of singing simply for the fun of it. Cary Sheldon is a singer, songwriter, and beloved Berkeley voice teacher with 30 years worth of grateful students. She has been playing and teaching in the Bay Area for the last 40 years. Her love for R & B music led her to be part of Zazu Pitts Memorial Orchestra in the 1980’s. Other affiliations include The Henry Kaiser Band, The Henriettas (a recreation of DeZurick sisters, a popular country music duo from the 1940’s), who appeared on Prairie Home Companion, and most recently her band DanceChant, a joyful community-inspired R&B band that encourages audience participation. She continues to be inspired by her love of singing in community. “Singing together with others is one of the greatest joys in my life.” Now in her 60’s, she returns to influences from her early life. Her grade school music teachers included John Langstaff, creator of the Christmas Revels, and the repertoire was based on the American folk tradition, including old English ballads, spirituals, freedom songs, and the popular folk and protest songs of the 1960’s. She hopes to inspire others to explore the depth of this material and rediscover the joy of community singing. Soprano Candace Johnson has led AMN’s Juneteenth Choral Celebration since its inception in 2020. The AMN community knows her through her commitment to the power of the Negro Spirituals tradition, but Candace has a deep connection to theater and to the music of the Broadway stage. A voice instructor at UC Berkeley for 17 years, in 2022 Candace also became the director of the University Gospel Choir. A lyric coloratura soprano, she crosses musical boundaries performing classical, jazz, musical theater, pop and gospel. She has sung on many stages, including Carnegie Hall and The Manhattan Center. Also a playwright and actress, Candace premiered her first one-woman show, Vox in a Box , in UC Berkeley’s Hertz Hall in 2018, which led to her becoming a resident solo artist at The Marsh theater (Berkeley/San Francisco). Candace has written and performed 5 full-length one-woman musicals. Her most recent show, Scat-ter Brain: The Music of ADHD , was commissioned by The Marsh in 2024 for its inaugural IFOYE festival of new works by women-identifying playwrights. Following an extended run, Scat-ter Brain was nominated by Broadway World SF for Best Solo Show of 2025. Please read our Health, Safety and COVID-19 Information Our commitment to our patrons

13cd652d-3e0c-440e-b80c-a153156a9205: A group meditation/authentic relating practice that explores what is coming up in the present moment as we relate to each other Welcome to a twice-monthly drop-in Relatefulness practice with Josh Rosenberg and Daniel Ricciardelli. Relatefulness is an exploration of what is coming up in the present moment as we relate to the others in the group. It is a close friend of relational practices like Circling™, Authentic Relating, and T-Group, with slightly more emphasis on group interaction and flexibility in how to express what is arising in the present moment. This is a mixed-levels event. Beginners are welcome and will be supported with tools to aid their exploration. Advanced practitioners will be challenged to find the next edge of their practice. We cap attendance for the event at 15 people. If you want to be sure to be able to join, purchase your ticket in advance! What We’ll Explore Through paired, small group, and full group processes, we will practice: Noticing and naming the content of our experience, including: our emotions, body sensations, and present moment reactions to others in the group. Noticing and naming the context of our experience, including: our assumptions, the norms of the group, and projections onto one another and society. Revealing our experience to one another to help all of us see each other and our broader social reality more clearly. Leading the group in the direction we want to go. This is a practice where all participants are invited to notice their desires for the group and to practice directing the group by embodying the kinds of expression they want to see more of. Why Come? You may be looking to: Cultivate more authentic, nourishing relationships, where you can be yourself and stay connected. Take your insights about personal growth and explore them in an interpersonal context. Set clear, compassionate boundaries instead of repeating painful patterns This practice helps to develop skills that support all of the above. Also, it's fun! What Not to Expect This is not a therapy session or group healing experience, although healing can occur. It’s a group exploration of what is arising in the present moment. This naturally tends to bring out more truth and love in the group, but there is not a particular goal or endpoint we are trying to reach. Here’s what NOT to expect: A space free of conflict or triggers. When people are open about what's coming up in their experience, things can get edgy sometimes! We don’t view being triggered as inherently negative, but rather a natural part of the human experience that can be rich to explore. We aim for a space where safety grows from honesty and genuine care, not from avoiding interpersonal conflict. To support this, we will establish some boundaries up front, such as asking for explicit consent before making physical contact with others. No enforced hierarchy of emotions. Beauty, awkwardness, boredom, anger, and joy are all welcome. Each experience has worth, and none automatically justify themselves as more important. Expression without attunement. We value honest expression, and we also stay attentive to its impact on others. This is a space for mindful connection, not expression at any cost. Facilitators may pause or redirect moments that move away from relational presence. Other logistics and notes Participants enter the space at 6:30 and we close the doors for the event at 6:35. Please arrive on time! We hope to see you at a future event! Feel free to reach out to jhrosenberg [at] gmail [dot] com or dbricciardelli [at] gmail [dot] com if you have questions about whether this event is a fit for you. More about the facilitators Josh Rosenberg (he/him) is a certified facilitator through the Relateful Company training program. He has hosted and facilitated weekly relatefulness sessions for small groups for several years while continuing to grow his practice through retreats and regularly engaging other facilitators. Josh loves exploring what's honestly coming up in the present moment in a group of people, and the novelty and relief it tends to bring. When he's not leading relatefulness sessions or at work, you may find him loving the heck out of music, movies, and comedy, participating in Michael Taft's meditation courses, or passionately following the New York Jets football team despite its many flaws. In his day job, Josh is CEO at the Forecasting Research Institute, a nonprofit aiming to advance the science of forecasting and increase its policy-relevance. Daniel Ricciardelli (he/him) has hundreds of hours in relational awareness practices of various forms, and is a certified Relatefulness practitioner through the Relateful Company. He draws from a decade of experience guiding men’s circles, performance dance teams, applied AI research, and meditation. Some recent inspirations of his are Ego Development Theory, madhyamaka philosophy, and Brazilian zouk. He is known for his steady, compassionate presence and calibrated relational risk-taking. He works full-time at the intersection of mental health and AI as a machine learning researcher.

He holds a PhD in sociology from NYU and is a postdoctoral fellow at NYU's Institute for Public Knowledge. Wolfe's debut book - Fires In The Night: The Earth Liberation Front, The FBI, And A Secret History Of Eco-Sabotage - tells the story of the Earth Liberation Front - a secret group of radicals who carried out the most audacious series of politically motivated arsons in American history - and the relentless federal hunt to bring them down. Publisher's Weekly said that the book "poses potent questions about the ethical boundaries of extremism" and that "readers will be rapt." Journalist Seth Harp - author of The Fort Bragg Cartel - said that it was "as riveting as any thriller" and that the story is a "forgotten prequel to 9/11 that couldn't be more relevant today." The author will discuss his book, the environmental movement more broadly, and the ongoing relevance of the ELF as the climate crisis grows more serious every day and the federal government seeks to quash any dissidence in an increasingly authoritarian manner. As a mindfulness coach, he specializes in secular, science-based mindfulness training in retreats, groups, corporate settings, and one-on-one sessions. Michael is the author of several books, including the bestselling The Mindful Geek, Nondualism: A Brief History of a Timeless Concept, and Ego (which he co-authored), as well as the editor of such books as Hardwiring Happiness by Rick Hanson and The Science of Enlightenment by Shinzen Young. 926ac336-7fd1-453a-a906-a3b35ec1c6c1: By midlife and beyond, the societal messages for women and non-binary people are clear: disappear or accept whatever life has wrought in their personal and creative lives. Two authors who span generations, Kate Farrell (Silent Generation) and Jordan Rosenfeld (Gen X), reject this notion completely. This workshop offers revised attitudes and innovative approaches to our writing and lives in midlife and beyond. Come prepared to discuss, write, and reframe how we think about creativity, feminine archetypes, and aging. Drawing on mythology, literary examples, personal stories, psychological research, and an exploration of the enduring power of feminine creativity (widely defined), Kate and Jordan crack open old ideas and lead participants in exercises to awaken our essential forces through challenging midlife transitions. You don’t have to be a writer, but come prepared to respond to thoughtful, playful prompts that ignite the power of your life's next chapter. Meet Your Instructors Jordan Rosenfeld is author of Writing Through the Pause: Mining Midlife for Powerful W riting , seven other books on the craft and process of writing including Make a Scene, How to Write a Page Turner , and The Sound of Story: Developing Voice and Tone in Writing , and three novels, with a fourth, Seeking Solace , publishing in ’28. Learn more at Jordanrosenfeld.net and jordanwritelife.substack.com. Kate Farrell is the author of Fairy Tale Heroine: Live and Write Her Journey, Story Power: Secrets to Creating, Crafting, and Telling Memorable Stories , and she founded Woven, an ongoing workshop platform using the framework of the heroine's journey for creative projects. Read more at woventales.net and katefarrell.net .

839b7fd7-5c91-4a0f-b551-3becff1458ee: Johansson Projects presents Land Figures, Nicole Irene Anderson’s second solo exhibition of landscape paintings and drawings with the gallery. Known for her haunting California landscapes, Nicole Irene Anderson renders subjects not as static portraits but as living atmospheres—shifting, flickering, and at times nearly dissolving into their environments. These forms become little islands unto themselves, bound not by topography but by the emotional weather of their surroundings. Her work stirs with an uncanny, near-hallucinatory stillness, drawing us into moments where the familiar becomes spectral and the personal, mythic. In Anderson’s world, the human condition is not a singular state but a diffuse, mercurial experience. Our disparate and illusory natures seek to know each other in the darkness. The artist’s subjects—sometimes solitary, sometimes accompanied—are lanterns in the fog. They search for connection, and occasionally, they find it in ways we do: in familiarity, in strangeness, in memory, and the mirrors of perception. Her work suggests that this kind of connection, fragile and radiant, is possible only when we open ourselves to the ache of vulnerability. To witness the illusion of stillness in an entropic universe. To describe Nicole Irene Anderson as simply a painter is to understate the force majeure she embodies in the studio. She mines the emotional terrain with an unrelenting commitment, refusing sentimentality in favor of something sharper, truer. Her hyperrealities are not polished simulations but cracked and flickering truths formed in the crucible of lived experience. They are a response to a world that often feels unreal—and a defiant claim that feeling, in all its terror and tenderness, is real. This is not escapism. It is a radical kind of noticing. I’d like to believe her singular ability to reconstitute contemporary landscapes—both internal and external —was born from her formative time here on the Central Coast. A terrain too stark and too honest to allow for illusion. There is a coastal realism that imprints itself on those who grow up alongside its fog-drenched cliffs and fractured light. It teaches you to see things for what they are, even when they hide. Anderson never stopped looking. Her paintings speak the visual language of that upbringing: attuned to absence, lit by empathy, edged with mystery. In the lineage of artists who collapse the boundaries between place, psyche, and spirit, Anderson is carving out her own topography—one that is deeply rooted, relentlessly curious, and wholly her own. By Charles Smith Land Figures runs March 13, 2026 to May 1 2027. An opening reception will be held Saturday, March 13 from 3-5pm.

Born in Novato and raised in Petaluma, Heath began singing at eight and was inspired by the Billie Holiday records in her mother’s collection. She spent the last two years of high school at Michigan’s prestigious Interlochen Arts Academy before acting studies in New York and a career as a working Shakespearean actor that took her from Florida to Beijing and all points in between. Upon returning to the Bay Area, Heath dove headlong into music, assembling a series of groups that would honor areas of early jazz that she wanted to explore and bring to audiences, from the Roma jazz of Django Reinhardt and the traditional jazz of the 1920s to the swing of the 30s and 40s and the Great American Songbook. For this night, Heath celebrates the legacy of Lady Day — particularly her collaborations with pianist Teddy Wilson in the 1930s — through music, storytelling, and visuals that immerse the listeners in the era, placing the songs in historical context that gives the timeless music a still deeper meaning. 7859e565-2dd5-4b24-ae26-072d0e446915: A jazz visionary of global proportions · Avishai Cohen is an Israeli jazz bassist, composer, singer, and bandleader, born on April 20, 1970. He is recognized for bringing the bass to the forefront of jazz and has received global acclaim for his work, including the prestigious Miles Davis Award at the Montreal Jazz Festival in 2023. DownBeat magazine has described him as “a jazz visionary of global proportions,” and Bass Player magazine named him one of the 100 most influential bass players of the 20th century. In late 2024, the French government awarded him the prestigious Chevalier of the Order of Arts and Letters. It is a recognition for artists, writers, or other individuals who have played an important role in the arts and literature, or in their dissemination. With this award, France recognizes Cohen’s significant cultural impact and contribution to the arts through his music and performances. Raised in a multicultural family with roots in Spain, Greece, and Poland, Cohen’s musical journey began at age nine with the piano. After his family moved to St. Louis, Missouri, he discovered the bass guitar, inspired by the music of Jaco Pastorius. He later returned to Israel to study at the Music and Arts Academy in Jerusalem, where he switched to the upright bass. In 1992, at the age of 22, he moved to New York City to pursue his music career. His early years in New York were challenging; he performed on the streets and worked in construction to make ends meet. He also studied at the New School and performed with pianist Danilo Perez’s Trio. A significant turning point came in 1997 when he was contacted by jazz legend Chick Corea after sending him a demo tape. For over six years, Cohen was an integral part of Corea’s ensembles, which were instrumental in shaping his musicianship and as a leader. Cohen’s solo career began to flourish with his first four albums released on Corea’s Stretch Records label, which showcased his unique blend of Mediterranean and Latin influences. In 2002, he founded his own record label, Razdaz Recordz. Throughout his career, Cohen has released a prolific and diverse body of work, exploring various musical styles. Cohen’s compositions have also been widely used in film and television. He composed the original score for the French hit film Le Sens de la Fête (released worldwide in 2017) – Directed by Acclaimed Duo Éric Toledano and Olivier Nakache and the documentary De Terezin au Kinderblock de Birkenau (2020) directed by Chochana Boukhobza. Avishai plays a significant role in the 2023 film “Tel Aviv – Beyrouth,” showcasing his talents not only as a musician ( composer of the original soundtrack) but also as an actor. Cohen both composed the original soundtrack for the film and made his acting debut, playing a character named Avishai. The original soundtrack was also released as a standalone album. His on-screen presence as an actor adds another layer to his multifaceted involvement in the project. Cohen has engaged in numerous collaborations with orchestras since 2015, such as the Brussels Philharmonic and Gothenburg Symphony, among many others, and also with the Metropole Orkest in 2025. In 2020, he collaborated with UK pop artist Gary Barlow of Take That. In 2025, Cohen continues to foster new talent, introducing a new working trio with Itay Simhovich on piano and Eviatar Slivnik on drums, and will be touring globally, performing with the Avishai Cohen Quintet and other engagements with Orchestras. His next album release is currently in the works.

bcb8a63a-ccc9-490f-a134-9043aaa004fb: Join local author Elaine Hsiegh Yu for a celebration of her debut memoir Ugly Dumpling, an Asian American coming-of-age story about growing up in poverty with a mother living with mental health issues, and about the redemptive power of love. Elaine will be in conversation with fellow Bay Area author Dr. Nancy Liu. About the book: When Elaine Hsieh Yu arrives in Hawai‘i from Hong Kong at the age of four, her family’s hopes for stability quickly unravel. Her father, rigid and demanding, drifts in and out of her life. Her mother, loving but volatile, is at times neglectful. From an early age, Elaine understands that adults are not always able to protect or provide. Ugly Dumpling follows Elaine ’s journey from growing up poor, Asian, and largely invisible in Honolulu and East Los Angeles to raising her children in Silicon Valley. She shares vivid memories of family, survival, and love, tracing a childhood shaped by public assistance and undiagnosed illness into an adult life spent trying to give her children everything she never had. Honest, emotional, and at times funny, Elaine ’s story touches on relationships across three generations, revealing how the past shapes us but doesn’t have to define us, and how the unexpected paths and broken pieces can become something whole and beautiful. About the Author: Elaine Hsieh Yu was born in Hong Kong and grew up in Hawai’i and Southern California. She went on to build a career in Silicon Valley after graduating from Stanford University with degrees in Electrical Engineering. She wrote her debut memoir, Ugly Dumpling , to shine a light on mental health and intergenerational healing within Asian American families. She currently lives in the San Francisco Bay Area with her husband, where they raised their two children, while continuing to care for her elderly mother. As an empty nester, she devotes her time outside her tech job at Apple to writing, keeping her houseplants alive, and socializing with friends, sometimes talking and laughing a little too loudly. About the conversation partner: NANCY H. LIU, Ph.D., is a Clinical Professor in the Department of Psychology at the University of California, Berkeley. Previously a Fulbright Scholar, National Institutes of Health Fogarty Scholar, and Consultant with the World Health Organization, her current work focuses on contextualizing evidence-based psychosocial interventions to increase their efficacy and effectiveness.
