6f86503d-3126-438b-978f-1d51aa22debe: The world is ending, and NOGA EREZ has a few suggestions. Keep the deliveries coming. Reach for Prozac or chocolate. Find reassurance in a fortune cookie. On ‘People, I hope you know the world is ending.,’ the first single from her fourth album, DUCK SEASON , she serves up familiar escape routes with a reassuring smile and a melody you can already hear a crowd singing back to her. Shopping, chemical comforts, compulsory optimism: everything we reach for to make reality easier to ignore is available here. And the song keeps smiling as the picture gets darker, capturing the spirit of a record where pleasure and unease share a beat, jokes land dangerously close to home, and even the most swaggering voice can crack. With the ingenious hooks, mischievous production and irresistible rhythms that have become the signature of Erez and her longtime creative and life partner, songwriter and producer Ori Rousso, DUCK SEASON may be their most accessible album yet. But it’s also the most personal and confrontational, balancing sharp social commentary with moments of vulnerability and compassion. Where 2024's THE VANDALIST embraced darker experimentation and the happy accidents of the studio, DUCK SEASON takes on a more cinematic quality, with each song creating its own vivid, sometimes unsettling world. Since Off The Radar , Erez’s 2017 debut, her exhilarating, genre-transgressive approach has won her a long list of high-profile fans, among them Missy Elliott, who appeared on 2022’s “Nails,” Billie Eilish, who called her “amazing,” and Robbie Williams, who dubbed her “The Queen.” She secured more still at Coachella 2026, her bloodied nose a swiftly viral representation of her and her band’s commitment. Throughout all this, she and Rousso have written their music and lyrics together, with their relationship sometimes inspiring their most intimate songs, a bond also explored in the new documentary, Noga . Now to the elephant in the room: Noga Erez is the world’s most successful Israeli musician, which does, inevitably, make her Israeli. For some, that may be reason enough to close the tab, but for those still here, there’s a more layered, revealing story. Born and raised in a country now viewed by much of the world with anger and revulsion, Erez has been outspoken about its leadership since the start of her career, both through her music and on the streets, protesting. She also asks uncomfortable questions about the hostility directed at her and fellow Israelis, including from those who, like her, oppose their government and its actions. What happens when nationality is taken as a declaration of belief, when someone’s birthplace speaks louder than anything they actually say or do? Having faced protests, cancellations, boycotts and death threats, Erez has lived those questions. They permeate DUCK SEASON – a title she’s had in mind since 2023 – and its exploration of identity, belonging and the struggle to be heard on your own terms. Those complexities are there from the opening track, “Shabbat,” which features Hichkas, the godfather of Persian rap. Originally from Iran, now living in London in exile, his homeland remains in conflict with hers, but hosts one of her biggest audiences. “ It’s the wild Wild West,” Erez announces, “ but we’re from the Middle East. ” This is a knowing declaration of nerve: when you come from the world’s most complicated region, it takes a lot to scare you. Even her choice of samples engages with that complexity: the track is named after Shlomi Shabbat, an Israeli of Turkish Jewish descent who’s sampled at its start, a reminder that her country is itself populated by immigrants and refugees. Throughout DUCK SEASON , Erez shifts from her immediate environment to the world at large, inextricably linking the two. On “Call Your Mommy,” she raps about sticking to one’s principles, while “Checkmate” tackles the forces seeking to control us, from the personal information we freely share to the societal pressures entrapping us. “PABLO” crosses borders, on this occasion generational, its painful observations stirred by her father and their country’s past — “ He calls it destiny / I call it history / We both make it repeat ” — while its playful rhythms are bolstered by military chants. If the title track, moreover, acknowledges despair, Erez mocks ideas of concealing this behind a stiff upper lip: “ He says, ‘Come run with me’ / I say ‘PTSD.’ ” On “My Car,” vibrant brass backs Erez’s refusal to let others claim ownership of her meaning: “ Don’t jack my car / Steal from me. ” Erez, however, is always as eager to point the finger at her own shortcomings as at anyone else’s. “Platinum Grill” skewers celebrity’s trivial escapism, recognizing its pull as much as its soul-destroying aftermath, and on “Hitchcock” she cautions, “Here comes the psycho!” to the ominous sound of a knock on the door as furious old-school beats and guitars pay tribute to Beastie Boys and Rage Against The Machine. She even plays a chilling femme fatale, amid Morricone-esque chimes and Hazlewoodian twangs, on the frankly murderous “November.” No wonder the sinister “Dollar Bill” reaches its sober conclusion: “ I’ll never heal / Till I finally come clean.” Few are as candid about drugs as she and her guest, Cara Delevingne. At times, too, Erez is blunter still. The militant “You And What ARMY?” scorns those whose intimidation reduced her identity to a passport, yet still it clings to an idealistic belief in a shared humanity: “ You can call me naive, but I’m right. ” The family portrait on the album’s cover gives that shared humanity an intimate frame: we belong to families, communities and countries, but those smaller units offer no exemption from a common fate. This conviction runs through a crucial verse in the song : “We human, don’t matter the side / Caught in a battle we don’t wanna fight / It’s heads doing the crimes / We the people we doing the time / Gonna send these oppressors a draft / You and your kids to the frontline. ” DUCK SEASON might as well have been called Open Season : to shoot first has become habitual, with questions as good as obsolete. By the closing track, “Human Season,” the implication is wider still: humanity itself is next in the hunters’ sights. Leaving us with the head spinning sound of Portishead and Radiohead on a malfunctioning carousel, she offers one final blast of unconventional honesty: “ God knows if I’m not real with you / No love / I’m so scared / Almost shit my pants / I do my best / It makes no sense. ” With an optimism bordering on – yes – naiveté, Noga Erez invites us to wake from the illusion we are separate, and to hell with the labels that keep us that way. “ We’re going down together... ”

d7e5007e-5a18-4dc5-8d26-90ab67c97fd5: Deconstructing Yourself is a weekly drop-in guided meditation (approximately one hour) plus Q & A with Berkeley Alembic founding teacher Michael Taft. Deconstructing Yourself is all about sharing the life-changing force that is meditation. We extend beyond any particular religion or technique in order to welcome any and all who are interested. Deconstructing Yourself strives to encourage, inform, and inspire your meditation practice towards ongoing awakening. Meditations are archived on YouTube here: https://www.youtube.com/michaeltaft108 Please arrive 10 minutes early. We do not allow any late entries for this event. Alembic founding teacher Michael W. Taft is a maverick meditation teacher, bestselling author, and podcaster. As a mindfulness coach, he specializes in secular, science-based mindfulness training in retreats, groups, corporate settings, and one-on-one sessions. Michael is the author of several books, including the bestselling The Mindful Geek, Nondualism: A Brief History of a Timeless Concept, and Ego (which he co-authored), as well as the editor of such books as Hardwiring Happiness by Rick Hanson and The Science of Enlightenment by Shinzen Young. He has often taught meditation at Google, worked on curriculum development for SIYLI, and is currently core faculty at Wisdom Labs, in San Francisco. Michael is also a featured teacher on the Simple Habit app, and an official advisor to the Therapeutic Neuroscience Lab. He was previously editor-in-chief of Being Human, and was the long-time editorial director of Sounds True. From Zen temples in Japan to yogi caves in India, Michael has been meditating for over thirty five years and has extensive experience in both Buddhist Vipassana and Hindu Tantric practice. Michael is a senior facilitator in Shinzen Young’s Unified Mindfulness system, and is a teacher of meditation groups around the Bay Area. He currently lives in Oakland, California, and is founding editor of the iconoclastic mindfulness meditation blog and podcast Deconstructing Yourself. NO ONE TURNED AWAY FOR LACK OF FUNDS. 5637a19b-d73f-4757-8465-094ba667e147: Meklit Hadero is an Ethiopian-American vocalist, songwriter, and composer, known for her electric stage presence, innovative sound and vibrant cultural strategy. A fixture on the Bay Area and global scenes, she makes her return to the Miner stage for the first time in six years. A 2019 Artist-in-Residence at Harvard University, she is a National Geographic Explorer and is co-founder and host of the podcast and concert series Movement. A Piece of Infinity, the latest album by Meklit, was released in 2025 on Smithsonian Folkways Records. It has already received rave reviews by Bandcamp, The Guardian, and AfroPop Worldwide, and has been featured by NPR Music, NPR’s Weekend Edition and the Recording Academy’s GRAMMY Global Spin. This album is an invitation to think, to love, and to groove, reimagining folk tunes from a multitude of communities and cultures throughout Ethiopia into jazz-inflected fantasies imbued with warmth and reverence. From songs of longing and love to children's riddles and original compositions, Meklit traverses expansive sonic ground that offers just a glimpse at the infinite complexity of Ethiopian culture. The album features guest appearances by harpist Brandee Younger and flutist Camille Thurman and was recorded at Women’s Audio Mission in San Francisco. Personnel: Meklit (guitar, vocals); Others TBA

10a1d682-289c-4fa5-904a-2062118f35c0: Ages 3.5 - 5 ABOUT WEBOP AT SFJAZZ We are thrilled to partner with our sister organization—Jazz at Lincoln Center—in launching the West Coast version of the acclaimed early childhood music education program, WeBop! The perfect preamble to our Family Matinee program and designed for youngsters between the ages 2-5 and their caregivers, WeBop at SFJAZZ is designed to introduce young children to jazz music and performance in a safe, welcoming and interactive setting. Classes are 45 minutes long and provide plenty of opportunities to learn, explore, and play. ABOUT THIS CLASS Musical activities for the Gumbo Group utilize dramatic play as a core learning element and provide opportunities for discovery and exploration through jazz. The multisensory nature of music—hearing, moving, touching, vocalizing—creates many entry points for children in this age group to be engaged and develop. They will learn to identify and repeat short musical patterns, explore important musical concepts—such as dynamics and tempo—through singing, listening, playing, and improvising with jazz tunes and stories.

a14aaf6c-5c10-40dd-bd83-2a2e62b03e8f: Creative expression is a way to integrate phenomenon and visions experienced in altered states of consciousness, whether they be meditative or entheogenic in nature. From the very first forms of mark-making to the caves of Lascaux to the works of Pablo Amaringo and Alex Grey, humanity has sought to understand our internal landscapes through visual expression. Alligator Lizards in the Air: Healing and Integration through Creative Expression, is a once a month chance to bring these experiences to life through two dimensional mark making. Art mediums from paint to colored pencils, crayons to markers, will be available for everyone to use along with paper and canvas. Krisztina Lazar will be your visionary guide in creativity and will help you realize your experience before your eyes. No art background needed for this class. All you need is an open mind and a willingness to explore. No one turned away for lack of funds. If this applies to you, please email hello@berkeleyalembic.org at least 48 hours before the event start. Krisztina Lazar is a visionary artist primarily working in oil paint, watercolor and drawing. She is a Mische Technique lineage holder, a mixture of oil and egg tempera painting invented during the Dutch Renaissance and revolutionized by modern master, Ernst Fuchs. This technique creates an opalescent under painting that the colors are then glazed over, rendering each painting out of light rather than shadow, bringing the images to life with fractal clarity. Utilizing this transformative style that she learned from visionary pioneer, Brigid Marlin, her current body of work explores painting a hybrid of Mische and Alla Prima to render hyperealistic sacred art. With these two techniques combined, Krisztina creates images of Pop Shamanism, portals and visions that speak to today’s cultural climate of the occult, magic, fantasy, psychedelics, meditation, pop, nostalgia, and the environment movement. Originally from Cleveland, OH, she completed her BFA at Carnegie Mellon University in 2004 and her MFA graduate degree in 2011 at the San Francisco Art Institute New Genres department. Her paintings have been exhibited in group and solo shows throughout the United States and Europe, most notably at the H.R. Geiger museum in Gruyere, Switzerland. She teaches her unique styles of painting to many students in group and private settings. Her work has been featured in multiple articles, galleries and book publications. She currently lives and works in Northern California.

ce5aefc0-4404-41c9-9d90-2ce2d1abc63a: A restless explorer who has collaborated with master musicians of Mali, interpreted the cabaret of Kurt Weill, and embraced the hard bop of Horace Silver, 2017 NEA Jazz Master Dee Dee Bridgewater brings a powerful new program she calls We Exist!, accompanied by a stellar rhythm section including pianist Alexis Lombre, bassist Liany Mateo, and drummer Shirazette Tinnin. Since she first gained recognition in the early 1970s with the great Thad Jones/Mel Lewis Orchestra, Bridgewater has thrived wherever she’s landed, and this show stands as a revelatory statement of purpose. Built as a “rallying cry” that connects past and present struggles, the program reimagines songs of protest such as Nina Simone’s “Mississippi Goddam” and Roberta Flack’s “Trying Times,” tracing the ongoing fight for justice and equality. Taking a cue from drummer and activist Max Roach’s landmark 1961 protest album We Insist!: Freedom Now Suite, the project confronts issues of racial oppression and civil rights while also championing female empowerment in a historically male-dominated jazz world. Bridgewater reinforces this message through an all-female ensemble, transforming the band itself into a living symbol of representation and change. It is a celebration of resilience, a platform for women in jazz, and a reminder—delivered with power and elegance—that music can still be a force for cultural and social transformation. Personnel: Dee Dee Bridgewater (vocals); Alexis Lombre (piano); Liany Mateo (bass); Shirazette Tinnin (drums)

9daaccca-83bc-4bad-97ca-1ef06e70e59d: 5Rhythms® dance is a profound medicine, offering a dynamic movement map into the vast, unexplored wilderness between our head and feet. Each rhythm - Flowing, Staccato, Chaos, Lyrical, and Stillness, is a gateway, a wisdom teacher guiding us toward greater presence, healing, and transformation. This event occurs every two weeks at the Alembic. In a Sweat Your Prayers®, we support your individual practice with the rhythms and your movement journey by dancing wave after wave with light guidance. People often leave feeling cleansed, grounded, more alive, and more connected to themselves and their deeper knowing. 5Rhythms® is for every body. Many have discovered that not having prior dance training is actually liberating! Bring your body temple and a willingness to be surprised by what's waiting to move in and through you. The dance will end around 12:15pm, followed by a closing circle until around 12:30-ish. We encourage spacious arrivals and unhurried departures. So plan your time generously: a little time to land, a little time to linger, and a little less rushing back into the busy world. This dance can be your mini-retreat for the week! Teacher Bio: Qibei is a 5Rhythms® teacher, mindfulness teacher, holistic healer, and Associate Marriage and Family Therapist, though no title could fully capture the many worlds she moves between. Her work bridges the clinical and the mystical, the tender and the fierce, the grounded intelligence of the body and the mystery of Spirit moving through human life. For over 20 years, alongside 5Rhythms®, her path has been richly shaped by Continuum Movement, Open Floor, somatic contemplative practice, and relational communication. Over time, these disciplines began weaving together into the way she listens, guides, and teaches. For Qibei, dance is medicine, prayer, and creative laboratory, a place where we can move beyond numbness, habitual defenses, and rigid identities we’ve learned to carry, and reconnect with our raw aliveness and deeper knowing. She believes embodied presence is what brings depth, vitality, connection, and magic into our lives. In her movement spaces, Qibei creates a trauma-sensitive and inclusive field for all bodies, inviting authentic expression and the dynamic interplay between body, heart, psyche, and spirit. Her music and facilitation are often described as exquisite, nourishing, and deeply transporting, guiding movers into inner landscapes they didn’t know they could reach. Qibei also facilitates women's circle and retreats. Learn more about her work at www.Qibei.be.

d5e3118e-eada-4736-932c-c2e313083599: This meditation and study group is based in the Insight Meditation tradition and its sources in Thai Forest and Burmese Theravāda Buddhism. To this foundation, we add exploration of Mahāyāna Dharmas particularly from the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā) literature and lineage. The group meets weekly online, and on fourth Tuesdays live at the Alembic. The focus of the group is on deepening in Buddhist liberation practice, and exploring the links between individual & systemic liberation in the form of social justice and collective healing. I bring a particular focus on working with the nervous system and resolving the symptoms of trauma, supported by devotional practice, study, and ethics as the basis of the path. All are welcome. Cost is $5, plus Dāna (pay what you can). This is the online version of the event: https://momence.com/l/GBhB5e6w Sean Oakes, PhD (he/him, queer, of Spanish/Puerto Rican and Northern European ancestry living on unceded Pomo land in California), teaches Buddhism, Yoga, and somatic practice. He has studied in Theravāda, Zen, and Vajrāyāna Buddhist lineages since 1993, including training as a monk in Burma, and was authorized to teach Insight Meditation by Jack Kornfield in 2010. His primary Buddhist teachers include Kornfield, Sylvia Boorstein, Gil Fronsdal, Eugene Cash, Kittisaro, Ṭhānissara, Ṭhānissaro Bhikkhu, Anam Thubten, and Chammyay Sayadaw (U Janaka), with whom he ordained as a bhikkhu for a Rains Retreat in Burma in 2002. He studied Haṭha and Vinyāsa Yogas with Alice Joanou, Rachel Shaw, Amanda Moran, and David Moreno, and taught mindfulness-based āsana and prāṇāyāma for 10 years. He performed for many years in music, dance, and performance art, including with Keith Hennessy’s Circo Zero, and was certified in Somatic Experiencing (SE) and Organic Intelligence (OI) with Steven Hoskinson, integrating the complex systems approach from OI in a distinctively Buddhist approach to trauma resolution. He received his PhD in Performance Studies from UC Davis in 2016, writing on extraordinary states of consciousness in Buddhist meditation and experimental dance. He teaches at Spirit Rock Meditation Center, East Bay Meditation Center, Insight Timer, and elsewhere, focusing on the integration of philosophy, somatics, and social justice discourse with the Dharma. Website: SeanFeitOakes.com
3c12c5e0-d913-4484-8a41-4329ac555e2e: Vacations’ fourth album finds the Newcastle indie rock quartet reaching new peaks and charting exciting new territory for themselves in the process. The follow-up to 2024’s sensational No Place Like Home adds new levels of warmth and texture to the group’s sound, drawing from the ornate chamber-pop of Weyes Blood as well as Beach Fossils’ gorgeously fuzzy rock style for inspiration. More than a decade into their career, Vacations’ sound continues to grow and mature, and Pursuit of Anything reflects the junctures the group have reached in their personal lives as well as the tightening bond that they’ve developed thus far in their incredible career. Pursuit of Anything arrives after extensive touring that followed No Place Like Home —a rigorous and wide-reaching schedule that included performances at Kilby Block Party and London Calling, as well as their own MATES festival (headlined by Vacations and featuring bands from Australia, the UK, and the U.S. curated by Vacations) in Los Angeles and late-night performances on Jimmy Kimmel Live and The Late Show With Stephen Colbert . “It got to a point where we needed to take a step back and look at our own lives,” bandleader Campbell Burns reflects. Indeed, as Vacations enjoyed a much-needed respite, life kept moving: Burns moved to L.A. briefly before eventually settling down in Brooklyn, bassist Jake Johnson and drummer Joseph Van Lier both got married (the latter also welcomed his first child), and guitarist Nate Delizzotti relocated to Melbourne. Amidst all this personal motion, Pursuit of Anything began to take shape, as Burns began writing the album in L.A. The band joined him for multiple sessions while in L.A. before Burns moved to NYC where he continued writing and recording in his apartment. The band reconvened for more sessions at Golden Retriever in Sydney to continue recording its ten songs. Burns then finished the album in NYC at Thump Studios and his apartment, along with multiple session musicians who were enlisted to help shape the record’s sound. Lyrically, Pursuit of Anything hones in on the growing pains of getting older, as well as how the ties that bind only grow stronger as a result of those opposing forces. “We're all going through a transitional period, and our lives are kind of starting to diverge in many different ways,” Burns says. “When Vacations started, I was adamant about it being a solo project. Over time, it became a band, and we've become so close. These people are my best friends—I've seen them go through so much, and we all help each other.” That close camaraderie led to Pursuit of Anything becoming more of a full-band than ever before: “In the studio, it’s all of us working towards the same goal and trying to get the best out of each other. There's a lot of love and respect that goes into everything, and it doesn't ever feel like work.” Adding to the creative pot was engineer Beatriz Artola, who Burns refers to as “The kind of person that you can trust to make changes, which goes a long way. It was like working with a mentor. I have so much respect for her, and she gave me a lot of self-confidence in my own production skills as well.” And Pursuit of Anything brims with easygoing self-confidence throughout, as Vacations make it sound easy to craft such impossibly pristine guitar pop. Ironically, the sparkling “Holy Grail” was directly inspired by a Zoom call with the band’s manager in which the quartet found themselves at a career crossroads: “We were caught in this catch-22 of needing to get into the studio so that we had a reason to keep going on the road. It’s about this idea that something that can bring you so much joy and fulfillment in life can also cause so much stress. But when you do figure it out, it's one of the most gratifying experiences you can have.” The album’s closing ballad “Lucky Forever,” which Burns describes as “me trying to write the most clichéd love song that I can while trying to be really earnest” and was directly inspired by his attending the weddings of Johnson and Van Lier. “I wanted to write a song from their perspective,” he recalls. “I don't really write love songs, and as a subject it's been incredibly overdone. But it was really refreshing to just write something that was so simple when it came to the intention.” The introspective penultimate track “I See Myself in You” was written with Frank Corr of labelmates Morning Silk, who became a friend of Burns’ following his move to NYC. “We’d get together and write, and we ended up with this lush arrangement,” he recalls. The song was inspired by a conversation Burns had with his parents in Sydney before flying back to New York City. He reflects, “I was going through something personal at the time, and they were there for me in a way that felt like I was talking to my best friends, because I was. My relationship with my parents has changed so much over the course of my life and it made me pause and realise how similar we are and our experiences. I also started to wonder if one day I’ll be in their position, having a similar conversation with my child.” Such moments tie in to Pursuit of Anything ’s larger thematic sweep, which Burns describes as “The coming-of-age that is going into your 30s while thinking about your younger self.” Fittingly, the spiky and spritely “Last Call,” which emerged out of his love for “short, catchy songs,” uses the titular closing time at a watering hole to represent the very real fear of time slipping away from your very fingers. “Am I not going to catch up?” he rhetorically asks while talking about the song’s broader thematic bent. “Am I just stuck wasting away doing things that are more trivial?”

1ad8c1a2-14bc-45e9-969d-380f0390a7e4: A group meditation/authentic relating practice that explores what is coming up in the present moment as we relate to each other Welcome to a twice-monthly drop-in Relatefulness practice with Josh Rosenberg and Daniel Ricciardelli. Relatefulness is an exploration of what is coming up in the present moment as we relate to the others in the group. It is a close friend of relational practices like Circling™, Authentic Relating, and T-Group, with slightly more emphasis on group interaction and flexibility in how to express what is arising in the present moment. This is a mixed-levels event. Beginners are welcome and will be supported with tools to aid their exploration. Advanced practitioners will be challenged to find the next edge of their practice. We cap attendance for the event at 15 people. If you want to be sure to be able to join, purchase your ticket in advance! What We’ll Explore Through paired, small group, and full group processes, we will practice: Noticing and naming the content of our experience, including: our emotions, body sensations, and present moment reactions to others in the group. Noticing and naming the context of our experience, including: our assumptions, the norms of the group, and projections onto one another and society. Revealing our experience to one another to help all of us see each other and our broader social reality more clearly. Leading the group in the direction we want to go. This is a practice where all participants are invited to notice their desires for the group and to practice directing the group by embodying the kinds of expression they want to see more of. Why Come? You may be looking to: Cultivate more authentic, nourishing relationships, where you can be yourself and stay connected. Take your insights about personal growth and explore them in an interpersonal context. Set clear, compassionate boundaries instead of repeating painful patterns This practice helps to develop skills that support all of the above. Also, it's fun! What Not to Expect This is not a therapy session or group healing experience, although healing can occur. It’s a group exploration of what is arising in the present moment. This naturally tends to bring out more truth and love in the group, but there is not a particular goal or endpoint we are trying to reach. Here’s what NOT to expect: A space free of conflict or triggers. When people are open about what's coming up in their experience, things can get edgy sometimes! We don’t view being triggered as inherently negative, but rather a natural part of the human experience that can be rich to explore. We aim for a space where safety grows from honesty and genuine care, not from avoiding interpersonal conflict. To support this, we will establish some boundaries up front, such as asking for explicit consent before making physical contact with others. No enforced hierarchy of emotions. Beauty, awkwardness, boredom, anger, and joy are all welcome. Each experience has worth, and none automatically justify themselves as more important. Expression without attunement. We value honest expression, and we also stay attentive to its impact on others. This is a space for mindful connection, not expression at any cost. Facilitators may pause or redirect moments that move away from relational presence. Other logistics and notes Participants enter the space at 6:30 and we close the doors for the event at 6:35. Please arrive on time! We hope to see you at a future event! Feel free to reach out to jhrosenberg [at] gmail [dot] com or dbricciardelli [at] gmail [dot] com if you have questions about whether this event is a fit for you. More about the facilitators Josh Rosenberg (he/him) is a certified facilitator through the Relateful Company training program. He has hosted and facilitated weekly relatefulness sessions for small groups for several years while continuing to grow his practice through retreats and regularly engaging other facilitators. Josh loves exploring what's honestly coming up in the present moment in a group of people, and the novelty and relief it tends to bring. When he's not leading relatefulness sessions or at work, you may find him loving the heck out of music, movies, and comedy, participating in Michael Taft's meditation courses, or passionately following the New York Jets football team despite its many flaws. In his day job, Josh is CEO at the Forecasting Research Institute, a nonprofit aiming to advance the science of forecasting and increase its policy-relevance. Daniel Ricciardelli (he/him) has hundreds of hours in relational awareness practices of various forms, and is a certified Relatefulness practitioner through the Relateful Company. He draws from a decade of experience guiding men’s circles, performance dance teams, applied AI research, and meditation. Some recent inspirations of his are Ego Development Theory, madhyamaka philosophy, and Brazilian zouk. He is known for his steady, compassionate presence and calibrated relational risk-taking. He works full-time at the intersection of mental health and AI as a machine learning researcher.

83128834-4935-4bb1-b3d4-58cdcf506be5: Darra Goldstein is the founding editor of Gastronomica and editor in chief of the Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Food Studies . The author of eight cookbooks, including The Georgian Feast and Beyond the North Wind: Russia in Recipes and Lore , she has won numerous prizes for her work in food, including James Beard and IACP awards. Her latest book, written with Cortney Burns and Richard Martin, is Cultured , a global compendium of fermented and preserved foods. Darra has consulted for the Council of Europe on using food as a tool for tolerance and diversity and has held distinguished fellowships in food studies at the University of Toronto and the University of Melbourne. She currently sits on the board of the Julia Child Foundation for Gastronomy and the Culinary Arts and is a member of the advisory “Kitchen Cabinet” of the Smithsonian National Museum of American History. Cultured - The only book on preserving you'll ever need! A vast and ambitious hardback cookbook featuring over 150 preserving recipes for drinks, condiments, snacks, and sweets. Organized by how long each recipe takes, there is something for all timescales―from quick pickles that are ready that day to methods that take weeks or months but can survive for years. Cultured draws on culinary traditions from around the world, employing techniques such as drying, canning, freezing, pickling, fermentation, salting, and freeze-drying. Making condiments like harissa and adjika, as well as staples and treats like kimchi, sauerkraut, preserved lemons, horchata, and pomegranate molasses to eat now and enjoy later has never been easier. The recipes are also accompanied by information on how to use these preserved foods to transform your cooking. Written by the authorities in the field, and filled with fascinating essays, stunning photography, and illustrations, this volume is destined to become the go-to resource for all things preservation.

bc35178b-d0bf-4f4c-a819-55998e588f22: Deconstructing Yourself is a weekly drop-in guided meditation (approximately one hour) plus Q & A with Berkeley Alembic founding teacher Michael Taft. Deconstructing Yourself is all about sharing the life-changing force that is meditation. We extend beyond any particular religion or technique in order to welcome any and all who are interested. Deconstructing Yourself strives to encourage, inform, and inspire your meditation practice towards ongoing awakening. Meditations are archived on YouTube here: https://www.youtube.com/michaeltaft108 Please arrive 10 minutes early. We do not allow any late entries for this event. Alembic founding teacher Michael W. Taft is a maverick meditation teacher, bestselling author, and podcaster. As a mindfulness coach, he specializes in secular, science-based mindfulness training in retreats, groups, corporate settings, and one-on-one sessions. Michael is the author of several books, including the bestselling The Mindful Geek, Nondualism: A Brief History of a Timeless Concept, and Ego (which he co-authored), as well as the editor of such books as Hardwiring Happiness by Rick Hanson and The Science of Enlightenment by Shinzen Young. He has often taught meditation at Google, worked on curriculum development for SIYLI, and is currently core faculty at Wisdom Labs, in San Francisco. Michael is also a featured teacher on the Simple Habit app, and an official advisor to the Therapeutic Neuroscience Lab. He was previously editor-in-chief of Being Human, and was the long-time editorial director of Sounds True. From Zen temples in Japan to yogi caves in India, Michael has been meditating for over thirty five years and has extensive experience in both Buddhist Vipassana and Hindu Tantric practice. Michael is a senior facilitator in Shinzen Young’s Unified Mindfulness system, and is a teacher of meditation groups around the Bay Area. He currently lives in Oakland, California, and is founding editor of the iconoclastic mindfulness meditation blog and podcast Deconstructing Yourself. NO ONE TURNED AWAY FOR LACK OF FUNDS. 69ba366d-690b-4bd6-8c42-d8320fc4d03c: “One of the strongest pianists of his generation” (DownBeat), SFJAZZ Collective pianist Edward Simon brings his latest and most expansive project to the stage. When Dogs Howl is an ambitious multidisciplinary project that blends jazz composition, Afro-Venezuelan percussion, dance, storytelling, and immersive video design into a unified performance experience. Created in collaboration with SFJAZZ and commissioned by the Creative Work Fund, the work centers on the journeys of Venezuelan refugees and migrants who travel thousands of miles across Latin America in search of safety, opportunity, and belonging. Simon combines a jazz big band with traditional South American instruments and percussion, creating a sound world that merges contemporary improvisation with Venezuelan rhythmic traditions. Rather than presenting migration as abstract politics, the project emphasizes lived emotional experiences: displacement, resilience, memory, and reinvention. Its unique strength lies in how music, projected visuals, and movement interact to create a cinematic narrative atmosphere. When Dogs Howl reflects Simon’s long-standing commitment to socially engaged jazz and cross-cultural collaboration and further elevates his status as a visionary artist whose creativity continually pushes beyond borders, genres, and restrictions. Personnel: Edward Simon (piano); Rafael Barata (drums); Others TBA

bf5ecd3f-cb1b-476e-b3f0-945bb006b1d3: Trevor has spent years hiding from the world. Ever since a childhood encounter left him with green, scaly skin, he’s become something of a local legend in Seattle, more myth than man. But on the night of Monster Fest, he decides to take a risk. A first date with his crush, Cary, pulls him out of isolation and into a city alive with possibility. When an unexpected encounter hints that the past may not be finished with him, Trevor is forced to confront the part of himself he’s tried to keep hidden. With an electrifying indie-rock score, Lizard Boy has become a cult favorite, celebrated for its originality, heart, and genre-bending storytelling. This bold, offbeat musical is a celebration of identity, connection, and the courage it takes to be seen.
e57f2dda-4987-4864-a526-3707c5736e07: A father sets out to build the perfect daughter. With the help of a scientist, he creates an AI version of Claudia, adjusting her life again and again in pursuit of something just right. But each new iteration brings unexpected results. The more he tries to control who she becomes, the more complicated she gets. By turns hilarious and deeply revealing, Chloé Hung’s Perfect Daughter explores the gap between expectation and reality, and the quiet heartbreak of trying to be seen, understood, and loved on your own terms.

c27df99b-397f-4e65-a8b5-d9edfef983bd: The March installment of Terence Blanchard’s UpSwing series presents the Paris-based singer and songwriter Gabi Hartmann and the brother and sister duo of flutist Elena and keyboardist Samora Pinderhughes, highlighting the rising generation of jazz torchbearers. Gaby Hartmann is an acclaimed vocalist who elegantly blends pop, jazz, soul, and world music, who takes audiences on “an enticing musical voyage that echoes the bossa nova sounds of Brazil, the Afropop of Miriam Makeba and the cool jazz of Norah Jones” (Montreal Gazette). Born in Paris in 1991, she studied ethnomusicology before captivating international audiences with her multilingual storytelling and velvet voice. Her self-titled debut earned praise and a Japan Golden Disc Award nomination, while performances alongside Melody Gardot elevated her profile. In 2025, Hartmann unveiled La Femme aux yeux de sel (The Woman with Eyes of Salt), an album steeped in intimacy. Born in Berkeley and currently taking over the jazz world, Elena and Samora Pinderhughes have each made indelible marks on the global scene as bandleaders and collaborators. Flutist Elena rose through the SFJAZZ High School All-Stars program to become one of the most in-demand musicians in jazz, working with Ambrose Akinmusire, Herbie Hancock, Chief Adjuah, Childish Gambino, Esperanza Spalding, and Milton Nascimento. The award-winning pianist Samora Pinderhughes has ingeniously combined jazz, neo soul, and hip-gop, working with Common, Robert Glasper, Lalah Hathaway, and Sara Bareilles. His 2022 album Grief was listed among the best albums of the year by The New York Times and Bandcamp. The pair recorded their first album together, Catch 22, in 2005 when they were 9 and 13 years old.

9343a997-c0d9-4d03-8924-18ec5b4112f2: Special Easter Weekend Celebration w/ Grammy Award-Winning Vocalist, Songwriter & Gospel Legend · This Easter, experience an extraordinary celebration of faith, hope, and inspiration as Yoshi’s proudly welcomes back gospel music legend Fred Hammond for a powerful holiday weekend unlike any other. Hosted by beloved KDYA radio personality Steven Parker , this special Easter and Gospel Celebration features two nights and four shows of uplifting performances filled with joy, praise, heartfelt worship, and unforgettable musical moments. Returning to the Yoshi’s stage, Fred Hammond will bring his signature energy, passion, and spirit-filled artistry to a night of soul-stirring music. Audiences can look forward to beloved gospel anthems and fan favorites, including "No Weapon," "You Are the Living Word," "We're Blessed," "Love Never Fails," "Make Me Like the Moon," and many more timeless songs that have touched hearts and strengthened faith across generations. A Grammy Award-winning artist, acclaimed producer, and master bassist, Fred Hammond remains one of the most influential voices in contemporary gospel music. His groundbreaking blend of gospel, R&B, soul, hip-hop, and funk has inspired millions around the world and continues to unite audiences in celebration and praise. Gather with family, friends, and fellow believers for a joyful Easter weekend filled with uplifting music, heartfelt fellowship, and an atmosphere of hope and renewal. Don't miss this unforgettable opportunity to witness a gospel icon live at Yoshi’s and create memories that will stay with you long after the final note. Celebrate Easter. Lift your spirit. Experience the music. Be inspired. Presented by KDYA Radio Host Steven Parker of The Steven Parker Show and Mark Elliott of The A-List Musiq Circle FRED HAMMOND For more than 40 years , music lovers around the world have known Grammy Award-winning artist Fred Hammond as a gifted vocalist, songwriter, musician, producer and arranger. But as his peers and supporters alike have so reverently declared, he is without debate the architect behind the creation of a phenomenon in Gospel music, Urban Praise & Worship—a genre of gospel music that did not exist prior. As a result, Fred Hammond has become one of the most respected names in the music industry! In Fact, Essence Magazine (2017 Collector’s Edition) names Fred Hammond in the esteemed list of the 50 Greatest Male Singers of All Time! Fred Hammond has been hailed as an Inspirational Music Icon whose music STILL reaches people from all walks of life. Chance the Rapper recently performed his remake of Hammond's hit song “Let The Praise Begin" (entitled “Blessing/Are You Ready") on The Tonight Show w/Jimmy Fallon. Jamie Foxx performed Hammond’s signature hit anthem “No Weapon” during his acceptance speech at the NAACP Awards and elaborated during an interview (on Jimmy Kimmel Live) about how the song had such an incredible impact on Quentin Tarantino, Kerry Washington, and the cast of D’Jango as they were shooting some of their most intense, heart-wrenching scenes. And in a recent Instagram post, Pop/Hip-Hop Music Icon Justin Bieber declared Hammond’s “No Weapon” to be his “…favorite song!” In 2019 , Hammond collaborated on 2 major music projects with Hip Hop music Icons— Snoop Dogg and Kanye West, who currently holds the #1 Gospel Album spot on the Billboard charts! Throughout his professional career, Hammond has maintained a reputation for excellence, and few gospel artists can boast of the consistency of sales, radio airplay, and concert appearances that Hammond has achieved over the course of his career independent of the cross-over boost. As a solo artist, founder of the pioneering urban group Commissioned , and his work with Radical for Christ combined, Fred has sold over 8 million albums, and these endeavors have made him a mainstay on Billboard’s Gospel Chart top 10. His previous release {Pages of Life} Chapters I & II exceeded Double Platinum status and held the #1 position on the Billboard Gospel Charts for over 15 weeks. His 2006 project entitled Free To Worship bombarded Billboard’s #1 position on the Gospel Charts and was hailed as one of the year’s best-selling gospel albums. Beyond Hammond’s individual success, his achievements as CEO of Face To Face Productions and the FHammond Music Label have placed him in a class by himself. Since their inception, Hammond has served as producer on more than 100 album projects, racking up numerous awards and nominations including the Grammy, BET, N.A.A.C.P. Image, Stellar, Dove, and GMWA Excellence Awards. His debut independent release entitled “In Case You Missed… And Then Some” sold well over 200,000 copies. Over the years, he went on to produce several other incredible artists. The Official Fred Hammond Website | Face To Face Productions

665daddc-f169-4d32-9edc-e3fd93ce3fd1: Throwin’ Bo’s presents: Thomas Dollbaum “The realest-deal storyteller in indie-rock today is the Tampa-born, New Orleans-based singer/songwriter Thomas Dollbaum, and Birds of Paradise is his most powerful and dynamic work yet. Following up his critically acclaimed Wellswood (Big Legal Mess, 2022) and Drive All Night EP (Dear Life Records, 2025), Birds of Paradise is a goodbye letter to lost loved ones and former selves. These songs find Dollbaum searching for acceptance in the transient in-between places: Florida’s pine flatwoods, backroads leading to I-95, where birds fly across the water. And even though the ghosts of his alt-country predecessors Townes and Molina are definitely present, on Birds of Paradise, Dollbaum emerges from their shadows–waving to the past, sounding all the more like himself. This moment–this album–is long overdue. Both of Dollbaum’s previous releases had taken way too long to record, due to circumstances out of his control, leaving him frustrated. And after having been away from his home for eight years, the place he had left was no longer the place he remembered, and the unchanging of the natural world felt like a constant he wanted to write about. With a sense of immediacy, he wrote Birds of Paradise in three months. Called up the musicians he trusted and admired the most–Nick Corson, Josh Halper, and Jake Lenderman–and asked them to meet him at Dial Back Sound in Water Valley, Mississippi with producer/engineer Clay Jones. They learned and tracked the album in four days, capturing lightning in a bottle, a sonic revelation Dollbaum’s writing has always been waiting for. “Big Boi” recounts the time high school-aged Thomas got roped into giving a couple (outside the Waffle House) a ride to pick up drugs at a pill mill. At a time in indie-rock when many singer-songwriters like to proclaim they’re Southern, Dollbaum knows it’s more complicated than that. “One day I’ll take you down to a place that you can never get out/ Couple splinters in the wall, nothing to brag about,” he sings steady and direct after realizing the mess he’s in. It brings to mind the short story “Samaritans” by Larry Brown, where the narrator is tormented for having a helping heart. Like Brown, Dollbaum miraculously examines entrapment with generosity. “Pulverize,” the album’s hardest and darkest rocker, is sorta like another short story, “Time and Again,” by Breece D’J Pancake. Both song and story are told from the point of view of a man plowing down the road, picking up strangers, trying to forget real awful things they can’t mention. Dollbaum was inspired by the time he tried to drive across Louisiana overnight but then, halfway, decided to turn around. In “Pulverize,” Dollbaum’s narrator is too afraid to look back. “You should have seen me/ out of Texas in the high moon/ Playing with God riding across the border cooped up/ in a hoopty to the promised land,” he struts. Lenderman harmonizes with Dollbaum on the chorus, “Pulverize this heart.” Dollbaum sings the next line alone, slinging his voice the highest it’ll be the whole album: “I don’t even need it.” And by the end of the song, he’s screaming with an intensity we’ve never heard before: “It’s fine, it’s fine, it’s FINE.” But it ain’t just grown men trying to move on in Birds of Paradise. “King’s Landing” playfully frolics from the point of view of little-kid-Dollbaum growing up near a little private airport. And he’s got big dreams of flying him and his folks outta there. “I wish I could take us from this town,” he sings. But knowing this dream is “probably a waste of time,” he suggests going home and watching “Judge Joe Brown/ And reruns of Cops episodes in our home town.” “I hope we catch one where the bad guy gets away,” Dollbaum offers some optimism, “Maybe he’ll steal a small plane/ Fly off to the everglades/ Build us a home out of water and snakes.” When there’s nothing else, survival and imagination are the same thing. With the help of Lenderman, Halper, Corson, and Jones, Birds of Paradise is Dollbaum’s hard-won breakthrough. Alive and echoing like the poems and short stories you can’t shake: coyotes howl, birds fly south, kids chase rabbits through the sugar cane, and cigarettes are four dollars a pack. Birds of Paradise reminds us where we come from–the things inside ourselves we’ve forgotten–we just needed Dollbaum to show us. Here’s how to look back without fear or shame. Here’s authenticity.” — Ashleigh Bryant Phillips Bandcamp | IG Support to be announced. DOORS at 7:00PM | MUSIC at 8:00 PM Tickets

014469de-8039-438a-9c85-8ea407452f1b: Spend Easter Sunday with the group PopMatters calls “An unrepentantly soul-stirring sound capable of transcending time and place.” Powerhouse vocalist Annie Caldwell and her husband, guitarist Willie Joe Caldwell, Sr., founded a family band to keep their children from performing in juke joints and blues clubs. But Annie & The Caldwells ended up following the kids, pouring gospel fervor into secular songs. Hailing from West Point, Mississippi, the septet delivers a glorious book of original tunes inspired by the Gap Band, Chaka Khan, Bootsy Collins and George Clinton, all filtered through their love of the golden age gospel groups like the Ward Singers and the Soul Stirrers. For this Easter performance they’ll be drawing deeply from their critically acclaimed 2025 gospel album on David Byrne’s Luaka Bop label Can’t Lose (My Soul) — a masterpiece that PopMatters says “blends gospel fervor and deep grooves into a triumphant, soul-stirring album that reaches for transcendence.” Combining soaring gospel harmonies with grit and street savvy, the songs summon the spirit back into the sound that gave birth to soul music. Personnel: Annie Caldwell (vocals); Willie Joe Caldwell Sr. (guitar, vocals); Deborah Caldwell Moore (vocals); Anjessica Caldwell (vocals); Toni Rivers (vocals); Willie Joe Caldwell Jr. (bass); Abel Aquirius (drums)
cd0ab944-7900-464f-9380-37d9f9476b08: Anba and Global Media Presents. After Alex in Wonderland and Alexperience, Alex returns to the global stages with ALLEXCITED, his third musical stand-up special. A three-hour experience that brings together comedy, music, personal stories and social observations, ALLEXCITED takes audiences through the many sounds and stories that have shaped our lives. Through timeless Tamil film melodies, the show explores music, culture and changing times. For the first time, Alex takes to the piano on stage, adding a new dimension to his musical storytelling. At its heart, ALLEXCITED is an invitation to stay curious, keep an open mind, find common ground in the many things that bring us together, and celebrate our shared humanity. Strictly for audiences aged 13 and above, please!

af193289-e4a3-43fd-841c-5a01f99f4344: Deconstructing Yourself is a weekly drop-in guided meditation (approximately one hour) plus Q & A with Berkeley Alembic founding teacher Michael Taft. Deconstructing Yourself is all about sharing the life-changing force that is meditation. We extend beyond any particular religion or technique in order to welcome any and all who are interested. Deconstructing Yourself strives to encourage, inform, and inspire your meditation practice towards ongoing awakening. Meditations are archived on YouTube here: https://www.youtube.com/michaeltaft108 Please arrive 10 minutes early. We do not allow any late entries for this event. Alembic founding teacher Michael W. Taft is a maverick meditation teacher, bestselling author, and podcaster. As a mindfulness coach, he specializes in secular, science-based mindfulness training in retreats, groups, corporate settings, and one-on-one sessions. Michael is the author of several books, including the bestselling The Mindful Geek, Nondualism: A Brief History of a Timeless Concept, and Ego (which he co-authored), as well as the editor of such books as Hardwiring Happiness by Rick Hanson and The Science of Enlightenment by Shinzen Young. From Zen temples in Japan to yogi caves in India, Michael has been meditating for over thirty five years and has extensive experience in both Buddhist Vipassana and Hindu Tantric practice. Michael is a senior facilitator in Shinzen Young’s Unified Mindfulness system, and is a teacher of meditation groups around the Bay Area. He currently lives in Oakland, California, and is founding editor of the iconoclastic mindfulness meditation blog and podcast Deconstructing Yourself. NO ONE TURNED AWAY FOR LACK OF FUNDS. aafeb669-2526-4e3c-90ff-55a0b59ef61c: “One of the most studied (and copied) saxophonists on the planet” (DownBeat), SFJAZZ Collective musical director Chris Potter is undoubtedly one of jazz’s leading lights and a highly engaged student of history. His newest album project, Alive With Ghosts Today, is a stirring set of compositions that explores the power and poignancy of abolitionist John Brown’s life and his 1859 raid on Harpers Ferry that preceded the American Civil War. Joining him on the Edition Records album, and for this performance, is a decidedly off-kilter septet that Potter describes as “a slightly unruly village band” including master guitarist Bill Frisell and a lineup featuring violin, clarinet, trombone, bass, and drums. Drawing inspiration from gospel, blues, African music, and the wide vistas of Aaron Copland, Alive With Ghosts Today captures the spirit of the era during a period of deep fracture in the country, when the battle for slavery and freedom reached a boiling point that still resonates deeply within the collective American psyche. An omnivorous artist who has fronted multiple ensembles and collaborated with a staggering list of music's greatest names, Chris Potter again expands upon his remarkable output with Alive With Ghosts Today — a project he approaches with heart and soul. Of the project, Potter says, “It’s a story that holds the complexity and tragedy of America in one moment. It felt important to engage with it now.” Personnel: Chris Potter (tenor and soprano saxophone); Bill Frisell (guitar); Others TBA

Teacher Bio: Qibei is a 5Rhythms® teacher, mindfulness teacher, holistic healer, and Associate Marriage and Family Therapist, though no title could fully capture the many worlds she moves between. 4cf17316-8558-44a6-8095-eb3cc4122c7c: Many of us work with psychedelics without a guide or with limited support to integrate these experiences. That can feel painful or lonely when we’ve had meaningful journeys (and also when we’ve had disappointing journeys!). Healing – especially from interpersonal injuries – deepens when done in community. The same is true of personal and spiritual growth. Even the most joyful experiences are best metabolized when witnessed. Together, we become a mosaic – a colorful and varied community, greater together than the sum of our parts. Mosaic is a psychedelic integration circle for self-identified women. Here, you’ll find a supportive space to integrate the lessons, challenges, and wisdom from psychedelic journeys so that you can apply those learnings to everyday life. Together, we’ll seek to understand our psychedelic experiences and make profound insights accessible and actionable. Please arrive 10 minutes early to get settled in. We’ll begin promptly at the scheduled start time and cannot accommodate late arrivals. Thank you for helping us create a smooth experience for everyone. This is a drop-in, monthly supported peer group rather than a psychotherapy group. We create space for sharing stories and experiences, receiving support, and forging genuine connections. Meditation, mindful movement, somatic practices, Internal Family Systems parts work, and creative tools are all part of the fun. Whether you’re new to integration or looking to deepen your practice, you’ll find a supportive community here. Note: You’re invited to bring an object for our community altar that represents some aspect of your journey. No one turned away for lack of funds. If this applies to you, please pay at the door. This event is a closed container. There will be no further entry after 2:15. Dr. Lyssa Menard is a psychologist, psychedelic therapist, and professor (Northwestern University Medical School) with specialties in Integrative Medicine, trauma treatment, and health psychology. She is the founder of Strategies for Change, a coaching and consulting firm promoting personal, organizational, and leadership change and has been a consultant to a wide range of media outlets, including CNN, New York Times, and WebMD. She brings this varied background to her integration groups, facilitating growth and change through a multi-media concoction of integrative therapeutic approaches (mindful movement, creative arts, somatic healing and embodiment, social connection, and spiritual ritual). Dr. Menard’s book, "Results May Vary: Hope & Healing through Psychedelic-assisted Psychotherapy" is scheduled for release in 2026. As a beneficiary of excellent (and also, sadly, lackluster) psychedelic treatment, she is a skeptic of the field, a critic when necessary, and a true believer in the healing possibilities offered by these medicines. She serves as an advocate for community and patient education and fights for legal access to psychedelics for health and healing. As a recent transplant to California's Bay Area, Dr. Menard spends a ridiculous amount of time at The Berkeley Alembic, cavorting in nature, worshipping the sun, and developing community. Learn more about Lyssa here: https://lyssamenard.com/ Read Lyssa’s musings on Substack: https://lyssamenard.substack.com/

33a9b578-fd25-4ed9-a55f-b1ccb2aa9212: Psychedelics can surface anything, including awe, insight, grief, trauma, even ancestral or collective pain. Without support, it can be hard to make sense of what happened, let alone carry it forward in a meaningful way. Yirah—often translated as awe, reverence, or a kind of holy trembling—is the feeling of standing at the edge of something vast, meaningful, and not entirely knowable. Psychedelic experiences often bring us right to that edge. This Jewish psychedelic integration circle offers a space to meet those moments together, within the safety of Jewish community and the container of Jewish teachings. Together, we make meaning of what we’ve seen and felt, and begin the slow, human work of weaving those insights into our lives. Please arrive 10 minutes early to get settled in. We’ll begin promptly at the scheduled start time and cannot accommodate late arrivals. Thank you for helping us create a smooth experience for everyone. Each monthly, drop-in circle includes grounding and intention-setting, a brief orientation, an experiential practice (meditation, movement, somatic work, or parts work), and small- and large-group sharing. This is a supported peer group rather than psychotherapy, designed to foster connection, reflection, and practical integration. Note: This is an affinity space exclusively for people who identify as Jewish—by heritage or conversion—including those who are part-Jewish. Those who do not meet these criteria will not be admitted. To support safety and connection in a time of deep division, we also hold a clear and intentional container: we do not engage in political discussion here. The focus is on integration, presence, and community. Whether you’re new to Jewish practice or finding your way back in, whether your journeys have been expansive, messy, or disorienting—you’re welcome here. Facilitator Bio: Lyssa Menard, PhD, is a clinical psychologist, psychedelic therapist, and professor at Northwestern University Medical School who specializes in trauma, integrative medicine, and what it actually takes to change. She’s been featured in places like CNN and The New York Times, but her real work happens in circles like this one—where people show up as they are and do the brave, uncomfortable, life-changing work of integration. Jewish by birth and in a more recent, intentional deep dive into Jewish life, Lyssa brings a deep respect for tradition alongside a willingness to question, wrestle, and reinterpret—in the long Jewish tradition of meaning-making. 50f1dff1-cd5c-4175-b259-befca12d9296: Topic and guest to be announced. The Chalice is a recurring psychedelic salon held at the Berkeley Alembic the first Wednesday of every month. Instead of the mainstream focus on clinical trials, legal frameworks, and psychotherapy, the Chalice will draw from the deeper humanistic wells of history, poetry, the gods, ethnobotany, humor, and mystery. We are less interested in fetishizing psychedelic substances or psychedelic experiences than in cultivating psychedelic culture and exploring what it means to be psychedelic people. This first half of this event will be streamed online. The co-hosts for Chalice are Erik Davis, author and Alembic co-founder; Maria Mangini, co-founder of the Women’s Visionary Council and old-school head; and Christian Greer, currently a lecturer on counterculture at Stanford University. The first half of each gathering will feature a talk or special guest interview; the second half of the evening is designed to develop the community, sometimes with breakout groups, story hours, and peer-to-peer discussion, and always with more questions than answers. J. Christian Greer, PhD, is a scholar of Religious Studies with a special focus on global psychedelic culture. He has held teaching positions at Harvard University, Yale University, and is currently a lecturer at Stanford's Medical School. He is the co-founder, and the co-chair of the Drugs and Religion program unit at the American Academy of Religion, and each June, he leads “The Psychedelic Universe: Global Perspectives on Higher Consciousness,” an intensive, 2-week seminar on the history of psychedelics, hosted on-location at the University of Amsterdam, Netherlands. Alongside his research, he is an organizer for the Order of St. George's Horse, a pilgrimage confraternity & book publisher. His latest books include, Void Machines: the Paper Shrines of J. Christian Greer is a collection of his artwork, and Kumano Kodo: Pilgrimage to Powerspots (co-authored with Dr. Michelle Oing) which analyzes the pilgrimage folklore associated with the rainforests of Japan's Kii Peninsula. Learn more about his work here: orderofstgeorgeshorse.com Erik Davis, PhD, is an author, award-winning journalist, and teacher based in San Francisco. His wide-ranging work focuses on alternative religion, media culture, the popular imagination, and the psychedelic underground. He is the author of High Weirdness: Drugs, Esoterica, and Visionary Experience in the Seventies (2019); Nomad Codes: Adventures in Modern Esoterica (2010); The Visionary State: A Journey through California’s Spiritual Landscape (2006), a critical volume on Led Zeppelin (2005), and the celebrated cult classic TechGnosis: Myth, Magic, and Mysticism in the Age of Information (1998), which remains in print. Davis’s scholarly and popular essays on music, technoculture, drugs, and spirituality have appeared in scores of books, magazines, and journals, and his writing has been translated into a dozen languages. Davis has spoken widely at universities, conferences, retreat centers, and festivals, and has been interviewed by CNN, the BBC, NPR, and the New York Times. He graduated from Yale University in 1988, and earned his PhD in religious studies at Rice University in 2015. He writes the online publication the Burning Shore (www.burningshore.com), and his next book is Blotter: the Untold Story of an Acid Medium (2024).www.techgnosis.com Mariavittoria Mangini, PhD, FNP has written extensively on the impact of psychedelic experiences in shaping the lives of her contemporaries, and has worked closely with many of the most distinguished investigators in this field. She is one of the founders of the Women’s Visionary Council, a nonprofit organization that supports investigations into non-ordinary forms of consciousness and organizes gatherings of researchers, healers, artists, and activists whose work explores these states. She is a visiting scholar at the Berkeley Center for the Science of Psychedelics, and Professor Emerita in the School of Science, Allied Health, and Nursing at Holy Names University. For the last 50 years, she has been a part of the Hog Farm, a well-known communal family based in Berkeley and in Laytonville, California.

8e8b07c1-00ca-4111-b112-1fe9a8ebb8bb: Saxophonist Sam Gendel and bassist Sam Wilkes are two of the defining figures of the contemporary Los Angeles jazz scene, known widely as members of drummer Louis Cole’s iconoclastic band Knower and for their groundbreaking duo project blending virtuosic instrumental playing with heavy electronic processing. A partnership at its most unpredictable in a live setting, they perform pieces from their newest album UNRELATED, and more. Over the past decade, both musicians have helped redefine the language of modern jazz, shaping a distinctly West Coast sound that merges improvisation with ambient music, hip-hop, experimental electronics, and pop minimalism. Gendel first emerged through his acclaimed solo recordings and collaborations with artists ranging from Moses Sumney to Vampire Weekend, developing a saxophone style that feels hauntingly intimate and radically unorthodox. Wilkes, meanwhile, has become one of the most sought-after bassists and producers of his generation, celebrated for his elastic grooves, adventurous harmonic sensibility, and deeply collaborative spirit. First meeting at the USC Thornton School of Music, they have built a body of work that feels both deeply cerebral and emotionally immediate. Their latest music expands even further into abstraction and atmosphere, transforming fragments of melody and rhythm into immersive sonic environments. More than collaborators, Gendel and Wilkes have become architects of a new musical vocabulary, influencing a generation of improvisers across jazz and experimental music alike. b072d3d1-a721-41cc-9b02-921cf1073a03: Lisa Mezzacappa is a San Francisco Bay Area-based composer, bassist, bandleader, and producer. Called “one of the most imaginative figures on the Bay Area creative jazz scene” by The Mercury News and “a Bay Area treasure” by KQED public radio, she has been an active part of California’s vibrant music community for nearly 20 years. Mezzacappa’s activities as a composer and bandleader include ethereal chamber music, electro-acoustic works, avant-garde jazz, music for groups from duo to large ensemble, and collaborations with film, dance and visual art. Recent projects include Cosmicomics , a series of compositions inspired by Italo Calvino’s stories about the origins of the universe; avantNOIR , a suite for sextet rooted in noir fiction; Organelle , a chamber suite for improvisers grounded in scientific processes on micro and cosmic scales; Glorious Ravage , an evening-length song cycle for large ensemble and films drawn from the writings of Victorian lady adventurers; and Touch Bass , a collaboration with choreographer Risa Jaroslow for three dancers and three bassists. Current projects include the duo B. Experimental Band which performs original compositions for improvisers bimonthly in Oakland, CA; and premiering in 2020, The Electronic Lover , an opera podcast created in collaboration with writer Beth Lisick. Mezzacappa has released her music on the New World, Clean Feed, NoBusiness, Leo, and NotTwo record labels, and her work has been supported on the national level by the MAP Fund, the Foundation for Contemporary Arts, the Aaron Copland Fund, and the Andy Warhol Foundation; and by Bay Area funders the Wattis Foundation, Zellerbach Family Foundation, and Intermusic SF. She has been artist-in-residence at the Cité International des Arts in Paris, Fr; Djerassi Resident Artists Program, Headlands Center for the Arts and the Banff International Jazz Workshop. She was a participant in the Jazz Composers Orchestra Institute, a program of American Composers Orchestra and the Jazz Studies Institute at Columbia University. In addition to leading her own projects in the US and Europe, Mezzacappa has performed as a sideperson with heroes such as Fred Frith, Marco Eneidi, Rhys Chatham, the Paul Dresher Ensemble, Mark Dresser’s SIM Bass Ensemble, Nicole Mitchell, Ned Rothenberg, Myra Melford, Vinny Golia and many others. These days, she plays often with Rob Ewing’s quartet SIFTER, with David James’ GPS, with the Nathan Clevenger Group, with Ian Carey’s Wood/Metal/Plastic, with Cory Wright’s Green Mitchell trio, and Randy McKean’s Bristle, in addition to the ongoing, lifelong collaboration duo B., with drummer Jason Levis. As curator, she programs the annual JazzPOP concert seres at the UCLA Hammer Museum in Los Angeles, now in its 15th year; and co-organizes the new Do-Over Music Series in Oakland, CA with drummer Jordan Glenn. Previously, she founded the live cinema series, Mission Eye & Ear, at Artists’ Television Access, co-founded the Monday Makeout creative music series in the Mission District of San Francisco with trumpeter Darren Johnston, and initiated the Best Coast Jazz Composers series at San Francisco’s Center for New Music. She also periodically hosts the “Festival-of-Us,” a festival celebrating Bay Area creative jazz and improvised music.

Starting as a prodigy, Jobarteh began studies with her brother, kora great Tunde Jegede, at age four and gave her first public performance on the instrument at London’s Jazz Café at five. She deeply immersed herself in western classical music studies at London’s Royal College of Music, touring the world with her brother’s acclaimed ACM Ensemble as a teen and sharing the stage with Toumani Diabaté, Oumou Sangaré, and the BBC Symphony Orchestra. Her beguiling debut solo recording, Fasiya, showcased her skills as vocalist and multi-instrumentalist, and her follow-up for African Guild Records, Badinyaa Kumoo, was voted Best Album of 2022 by Songlines. 6f170421-2749-4f83-9879-4987c09db88d: October Theme: “Broadway and Show Tunes” There’s nothing that brings people together better than singing our favorite songs. It recalls summer nights around the campfire: someone strumming the guitar and all singing a mix of folk music, familiar songs we heard on the radio, and occasional new songs that someone shares. Nobody has to worry about whether you know the songs or can sing like a pro. This is our chance to share the joy of singing simply for the fun of it. Cary Sheldon is a singer, songwriter, and beloved Berkeley voice teacher with 30 years worth of grateful students. She has been playing and teaching in the Bay Area for the last 40 years. Her love for R & B music led her to be part of Zazu Pitts Memorial Orchestra in the 1980’s. Other affiliations include The Henry Kaiser Band, The Henriettas (a recreation of DeZurick sisters, a popular country music duo from the 1940’s), who appeared on Prairie Home Companion, and most recently her band DanceChant, a joyful community-inspired R&B band that encourages audience participation. She continues to be inspired by her love of singing in community. “Singing together with others is one of the greatest joys in my life.” Now in her 60’s, she returns to influences from her early life. Her grade school music teachers included John Langstaff, creator of the Christmas Revels, and the repertoire was based on the American folk tradition, including old English ballads, spirituals, freedom songs, and the popular folk and protest songs of the 1960’s. She hopes to inspire others to explore the depth of this material and rediscover the joy of community singing. Soprano Candace Johnson has led AMN’s Juneteenth Choral Celebration since its inception in 2020. The AMN community knows her through her commitment to the power of the Negro Spirituals tradition, but Candace has a deep connection to theater and to the music of the Broadway stage. A voice instructor at UC Berkeley for 17 years, in 2022 Candace also became the director of the University Gospel Choir. A lyric coloratura soprano, she crosses musical boundaries performing classical, jazz, musical theater, pop and gospel. She has sung on many stages, including Carnegie Hall and The Manhattan Center. Also a playwright and actress, Candace premiered her first one-woman show, Vox in a Box , in UC Berkeley’s Hertz Hall in 2018, which led to her becoming a resident solo artist at The Marsh theater (Berkeley/San Francisco). Candace has written and performed 5 full-length one-woman musicals. Her most recent show, Scat-ter Brain: The Music of ADHD , was commissioned by The Marsh in 2024 for its inaugural IFOYE festival of new works by women-identifying playwrights. 4f0e4b35-4c20-4d57-a4c1-81d60fd4da3d: A group meditation/authentic relating practice that explores what is coming up in the present moment as we relate to each other Welcome to a twice-monthly drop-in Relatefulness practice with Josh Rosenberg and Daniel Ricciardelli. Relatefulness is an exploration of what is coming up in the present moment as we relate to the others in the group. It is a close friend of relational practices like Circling™, Authentic Relating, and T-Group, with slightly more emphasis on group interaction and flexibility in how to express what is arising in the present moment. This is a mixed-levels event. Beginners are welcome and will be supported with tools to aid their exploration. Advanced practitioners will be challenged to find the next edge of their practice. We cap attendance for the event at 15 people. If you want to be sure to be able to join, purchase your ticket in advance! What We’ll Explore Through paired, small group, and full group processes, we will practice: Noticing and naming the content of our experience, including: our emotions, body sensations, and present moment reactions to others in the group. Noticing and naming the context of our experience, including: our assumptions, the norms of the group, and projections onto one another and society. Revealing our experience to one another to help all of us see each other and our broader social reality more clearly. Leading the group in the direction we want to go. This is a practice where all participants are invited to notice their desires for the group and to practice directing the group by embodying the kinds of expression they want to see more of. Why Come? You may be looking to: Cultivate more authentic, nourishing relationships, where you can be yourself and stay connected. Take your insights about personal growth and explore them in an interpersonal context. Set clear, compassionate boundaries instead of repeating painful patterns This practice helps to develop skills that support all of the above. Also, it's fun! What Not to Expect This is not a therapy session or group healing experience, although healing can occur. It’s a group exploration of what is arising in the present moment. This naturally tends to bring out more truth and love in the group, but there is not a particular goal or endpoint we are trying to reach. Here’s what NOT to expect: A space free of conflict or triggers. When people are open about what's coming up in their experience, things can get edgy sometimes! We don’t view being triggered as inherently negative, but rather a natural part of the human experience that can be rich to explore. We aim for a space where safety grows from honesty and genuine care, not from avoiding interpersonal conflict. To support this, we will establish some boundaries up front, such as asking for explicit consent before making physical contact with others. No enforced hierarchy of emotions. Beauty, awkwardness, boredom, anger, and joy are all welcome. Each experience has worth, and none automatically justify themselves as more important. Expression without attunement. We value honest expression, and we also stay attentive to its impact on others. This is a space for mindful connection, not expression at any cost. Facilitators may pause or redirect moments that move away from relational presence. Other logistics and notes Participants enter the space at 6:30 and we close the doors for the event at 6:35. Please arrive on time! We hope to see you at a future event! Feel free to reach out to jhrosenberg [at] gmail [dot] com or dbricciardelli [at] gmail [dot] com if you have questions about whether this event is a fit for you. More about the facilitators Josh Rosenberg (he/him) is a certified facilitator through the Relateful Company training program. He has hosted and facilitated weekly relatefulness sessions for small groups for several years while continuing to grow his practice through retreats and regularly engaging other facilitators. Josh loves exploring what's honestly coming up in the present moment in a group of people, and the novelty and relief it tends to bring. When he's not leading relatefulness sessions or at work, you may find him loving the heck out of music, movies, and comedy, participating in Michael Taft's meditation courses, or passionately following the New York Jets football team despite its many flaws. In his day job, Josh is CEO at the Forecasting Research Institute, a nonprofit aiming to advance the science of forecasting and increase its policy-relevance. Daniel Ricciardelli (he/him) has hundreds of hours in relational awareness practices of various forms, and is a certified Relatefulness practitioner through the Relateful Company. He draws from a decade of experience guiding men’s circles, performance dance teams, applied AI research, and meditation. Some recent inspirations of his are Ego Development Theory, madhyamaka philosophy, and Brazilian zouk. He is known for his steady, compassionate presence and calibrated relational risk-taking. He works full-time at the intersection of mental health and AI as a machine learning researcher.
